title: Remark
body_md:
A three-dimensional fault-tolerant cellular automaton cannot be built to
arbitrary size in the physical space.
Indeed, there will be an (inherently irreversible) error-correcting
operation on the average in every constant number of steps in each cell.
This will produce a steady flow of heat from each cell that needs
therefore a separate escape route for each cell.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Several methods have emerged that help managing the complexity of a large
construction but the following two are the most important.
 \begin{itemize}
  \item 
  A number of ``interface'' concepts is introduced (generalized
simulation, generalized cellular automaton) helping to separate the
levels of the infinite hierarchy, and making it possible to speak
meaningfully of a single pair of adjacent levels.

  \item
  Though the construction is large, its problems are presented one at
a time.
  For example, the messiest part of the self-stabilization is the so-called
Attribution Lemma, showing how after a while all cells can be attributed to
some large organized group (colony), and thus no ``debris'' is in the way
of the creation of new colonies.
  This lemma relies mainly on the Freeze and Decay rules, and will be
proved before introducing many other major rules.
  Other parts of the construction that are not possible to ignore are
used only through ``interface conditions'' (specifications).
 \end{itemize}
  
  We believe that the new result and the new method of presentation
will serve as a firm basis for other new results.
  An example of a problem likely to yield to the new framework is the
\emph{growth rate of the relaxation time} as a function of the size of a
finite cellular automaton.
  At present, the relaxation time of all known cellular automata either
seems to be bounded (ergodic case) or grows exponentially.
  We believe that our constructions will yield examples for other,
intermediate growth rates.

name: method simplification

label: eq:lem
title: Notation
body_md:
Let \( \mathbb{R} \) be the set of real numbers, and
 \( \mathbb{Z}_{m} \)\gloprocz.cap.z@\( \mathbb{Z}_{m} \).)))  
the set of remainders modulo \( m \).
For \( m=\infty \), this is the set \( \mathbb{Z} \) of integers.

We will use the notation
\begin{align}\label{eq:lem}
   f(n)\stackrel{{}_*}{<} g(n)
\end{align}
for what usually is written as \( f(n)=O(g(n)) \): that is for the fact that \( f(n)\le c g(n) \)
for some constant \( c \).
We write \( f(n)\stackrel{{}_*}{=} g(n) \) if \( f(n)\stackrel{{}_*}{<} g(n) \) and \( g(n)\le f(n) \).

The standard mathematical notation for open
intervals and for pairs is the same; we hope that the context will make the
meaning always clear.
We will use the same notation for intervals of integers as for those of real
numbers: the context 
will make it clear, whether \( [a,b] \) or \( [a,b]\cap \mathbb{Z} \) is
understood.
Given a set \( A \) of space or space-time and a real number \( c \), we write
 \[
  c A = \mathopen\{\verythinmathskipcv : v\in A\mskip 1mu\mathclose\},
 \]
and \( \overline{A} \) for its closure: for example, \( \overline{(a,b]}=[a,b] \).
Given two space-time sets \( A,B \), we denote
 \begin{align}\label{eq:set-sum}
 A+B = \mathopen\{\verythinmathskipa+b : a\in A,b\in B\mskip 1mu\mathclose\}.
 \end{align}
 
Some lists of assertions are denoted by
(a), (b), \( \dots \) and some by (1), (2), \( \dots \).
The attempted convention is that for a 
list properties that all hold or are required (conjunction) the
items are labeled with (a),(b), \( \dots \) while if the list is a list of
several possible cases (disjunction) then the items are labeled with (1),
(2), \( \dots \).

Maxima and minima will sometimes be denoted by \( \vee \) and
\( \wedge \)\gloproc"+@\( \vee,\wedge \).))).
  We will write \( \log \)\gloproclog@\( \log \).))) for \( \log_{2} \).
  For two strings \( u,v \), we will denote by 
\gloproc"+@\( \sqcup \).)))
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:concat}
   u\sqcup v
 \end{equation}
  their concatenation.

label: def:space
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:space}
  The set \( {\Lambda} \)\gloprocc.cap@\( {\Lambda} \).))) of
 \emph{sites}\index{site} has the form \( \mathbb{Z}_{m} \) for finite or infinite \( m \).
This will mean that in the finite case, we take \emph{periodic boundary
conditions}.
In a space-time vector \( (x,t) \), we will always write the space coordinate
first.
For a space-time set \( E \), we will denote its space- and time projections
by \gloprocp.greek@\( \boldsymbol{\pi}_{\text{s}}, \boldsymbol{\pi}_{\text{t}} \).)))
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:proj}
 \boldsymbol{\pi}_{\text{s}} E, \boldsymbol{\pi}_{\text{t}} E
 \end{equation}
respectively.
We will have a finite set \( {\mathbb{S}} \)\gloprocs.cap.s@\( {\mathbb{S}} \).))) of states, the potential
states of each site.
A \emph{configuration}\index{configuration} is a function
 \gloprocx.greek@\( \xi(x) \).)))
 \[ 
   \xi(x)
 \]
  for \( x\in{\Lambda} \).
Here, \( \xi(x) \) is the state of site \( x \).
head: environment
name: Space and states

label: def:space-time
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:space-time}
The time of work of our cellular automata will be the interval
\( \left[0,\infty\right) \).
  Our \emph{space-time} is given by 
 \[
 {\Lambda}\times\left[0,\infty\right).
 \]
A \emph{history}\index{history} is a
space-time function \( \eta(x,t) \)\gloprocy.greek.func@\( \eta(x,t) \).))) which for each \( t \)
defines a configuration.
If in a history \( \eta \) we have \( \eta(x,v)=s_{2} \) and
\( \eta(x,t)=s_{1}\ne s_{2} \) for all \( t<v \) sufficiently close to \( v \) then we
can say that there was a
\emph{switch}\index{switch} from state \( s_{1} \) to state \( s_{2} \) at time
\( v \).
For ordinary discrete-time cellular automata, we allow only histories
in which all switching times are natural numbers
\( 0,1,2,\dots \).
The time 0 is considered a switching time.
If there is an \( \varepsilon \) such that \( \eta(c,t) \) is constant for
\( a-\varepsilon<t<a \) then this constant value will be denoted by
 \gloproc-@\( \eta(c, a-) \).)))
 \begin{equation} \label{eq:a.minus} 
  \eta(c, a-).
 \end{equation}
The \emph{subconfiguration} \( \xi(D') \) of a configuration \( \xi \)
defined on \( D\supseteq D' \) is the restriction of \( \xi \) to \( D' \).
Sometimes, we write
 \[
  \eta(V)
 \]
 for the sub-configuration over the space-time set \( V \).

label: eq:trans
title: Definition
body_md:
A
 \emph{deterministic cellular automaton}\index{cellular automaton!deterministic} 
\gloprocca@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}, {\Lambda}) \).))) 
 \[
   \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}, {\Lambda}).
 \]
  is determined by a   transition function\index{transition function}
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}:{\mathbb{S}}^{3}\to{\mathbb{S}} \)\gloproctr@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}, \overline{\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}} \).))) and the set \( {\Lambda} \) of
sites.
We will omit \( {\Lambda} \) from the notation when it is obvious from the
context.
A history \( \eta \) is a
\emph{trajectory}\index{trajectory!deterministic cellular automaton} of this
automaton if 
 \[
   \eta(x,t)=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}(\eta(x-1,t-1), \eta(x,t-1), \eta(x+1,t-1))
 \]
holds for all \( x,t \) with \( t>0 \).
For a history \( \eta \) let us write
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:trans}
   \overline{\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}}(\eta, x,t)=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}(\eta(x-1,t-1), \eta(x,t-1), \eta(x+1,t-1))
 \end{equation}
for the ``intended'' value of \( \eta(x,t) \).
head: environment
name: Deterministic cellular automata

title: Definition
body_md:
We will deal, from now on, only with cellular automata in which the set
\( {\mathbb{S}} \) of local states consists of binary strings of some fixed length
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Cap\/}}}={\lVert {\mathbb{S}}\rVert} \)\gloproc"|@\( {\lVert {\mathbb{S}}\rVert} \).))) called the
\emph{capacity}\index{capacity} of the sites.
Thus, if the automaton has 16 possible states then its states can be
considered binary strings of length 4.
head: environment
name: Capacity

label: def:fields
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:fields}
Nonempty subsets of the set \( \mathopen\{0,\dots,{\lVert {\mathbb{S}}\rVert}-1\mathclose\} \) will be called
 \emph{fields}\index{field}.
Some of these subsets will have special names.
Let \gloprocall@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{All\/}}}} \).)))
 \[
   \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{All\/}}}} = \mathopen\{0,\dots,{\lVert {\mathbb{S}}\rVert}-1\mathclose\}.
 \]
If \( s=\mathopen(\verythinmathskips(i) : i\in\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{All\/}}}}\mskip 1mu\mathclose) \) is a bit string and \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}=\mathopen\{i_{1},\dots,i_{k}\mathclose\} \)
is a field with \( i_{j}<i_{j+1} \) then we will write \gloproc.@\( s.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}} \).)))
 \[
   s.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}=\mathopen( s(i_{1}),\dots,s(i_{k})\mathclose)
 \]
 for the bit string that is called \emph{field} \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}} \) of the state.
 The field consisting of the bits \( s(i),s(i+1),\dots,s(j-1) \) of the state will be
 denoted
 \begin{align}\label{eq:F[i:j]}
   \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}[i\mathord{:} j].
 \end{align}
The array obtained from joining 
the same fields (say the Mail field) of all the different cells is called 
a \emph{track}\index{track}, (say the Mail track).
(The terminology recalls tracks of a magnetic tape.)
We will generally define fields that 
are either disjoint or contained in each other (but there may be some
exceptions.)
We will call the number of bits \( |\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}| \) in a field its \( \emph{width} \), and
and the proportion \( |F|/\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Cap\/}}} \) its \emph{relative width}.
The width and relative width of a \emph{track} is defined to be the same as that of the
corresponding field.
head: environment
name: Fields

title: Example
body_md:
If the capacity is 12 we could subdivide the interval \( [0,11] \) into
subintervals of lengths 2,2,1,1,2,4 respectively and call these fields
the input, output, mail coming from left, mail coming from right,
memory and workspace.
  We can denote these as
 \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Input\/}}}} \)\gloprocinput@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Input\/}}}} \).))),
 \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Output\/}}}} \)\gloprocoutput@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Output\/}}}} \).))),
 \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Mail\/}}}}_{j} \)\gloprocmail@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Mail\/}}}} \).))) (\( j=-1,1 \)),
 \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Work\/}}}} \)\gloprocwork@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Work\/}}}} \).))) and
 \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Memory\/}}}} \)\gloprocmemory@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Memory\/}}}} \).))).
  If \( s \) is a state then \( s.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Input\/}}}} \) denotes the first two bits of \( s \),
\( s.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Mail\/}}}}_{1} \) means the sixth bit of \( s \), etc.
Treating these fields differently means we may impose some useful
restrictions on the transition function.
We might require the following, calling \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Mail\/}}}}_{-1} \) the ``right-directed
mail field'':
 \begin{quote}
  The information in \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Mail\/}}}}_{-1} \) moves always to the right.
  More precisely, in a trajectory \( \eta \), the only part of the state
\( \eta(x,t) \) that depends on the state \( \eta(x-1,t-1) \) of the left
neighbor is the right-directed mail field \( \eta(x,t).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Mail\/}}}}_{-1} \).
  This field, on the other hand, depends only on the right-directed
mail field of the left neighbor and the workspace field
\( \eta(x,t-1).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Work\/}}}} \).
  The memory depends only on the workspace.
 \end{quote}
  Confining ourselves to computations that are structured in a similar
way make reasoning about them in the presence of faults much easier.
  Indeed, in such a scheme, the effects of a fault can propagate only
through the mail fields and can affect the memory field only if the
workspace field's state allows it.

body_md:
A \emph{random history}\index{history!random} is a pair
\( (\mu,\eta) \)\gloprocm.greek@\( \mu \).))) where \( \mu \) is a probability measure over some
measurable space\index{measurable space}
 \( (\Omega,\mathcal{A}) \)\gloproco.greek@\( \Omega,\omega \).)))\gloproca.cap@\( \mathcal{A},\mathcal{A}(W),\mathcal{A}_{t} \).)))
 together with a measurable function \( \eta(x,t,\omega) \)
 which is a history for every value of \( \omega\in\Omega \).
We will generally omit \( \omega \) from the arguments of \( \eta \).
When we omit the mention of \( \mu \) we will use \( \operatorname{\mathsf P} \)\gloprocprob@\( \operatorname{\mathsf P} \).)))
to denote it.
If it does not lead to confusion, for some property of the form
\( \mathopen\{\mskip 1mu\eta\in R\mskip 1mu\mathclose\} \), the quantity
 \( \mu\mathopen\{\mskip 1mu\omega : \eta(\cdot,\cdot,\omega)\in R\mskip 1mu\mathclose\} \) will be written as usual, as
 \[
   \mu\mathopen\{\mskip 1mu\eta\in R\mskip 1mu\mathclose\} .
 \]

label: def:events
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:events}
 A function \( f(\eta) \) with values 0, 1 (that is an indicator function) and
measurable in the \( \sigma \)-algebra \( \mathcal{A} \) will be called an
 \emph{event function}\index{event function}  over \( \mathcal{A} \).
Let \( W \) be any subset of space-time that is the union of some rectangles.
  Then 
 \[
  \mathcal{A}(W)
 \]
  denotes the \( \sigma \)-algebra generated by events of the form
 \[
  \mathopen\{\mskip 1mu\eta(x,t)=s \text{\rmfamily\mdseries\upshape{ for }} t_{1}\le t < t_{2}\mskip 1mu\mathclose\}
 \]
 for \( s\in{\mathbb{S}} \), \( (x,t_{i})\in W \).
head: environment
name: Events

label: def:filtration
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:filtration}
For all times \( t \), we assume the existence of a \( \sigma \)-algebra
 \[
  \mathcal{A}_{t} \supseteq \mathcal{A}({\Lambda}\times[0,t]),\quad \mathcal{A}_{<t}=\bigcup_{u<t} \mathcal{A}_{u}.
 \]
The system \( \{\mathcal{A}_{t}\} \) is required to be increasing:
 \[
  t < u \Rightarrow \mathcal{A}_{t} \subseteq \mathcal{A}_{u}.
 \]
The function \( t\mapsto\mathcal{A}_{t} \) is our \emph{filtration}.
head: environment
name: Filtration

title: Example
body_md: The system \( t\mapsto\mathcal{A}({\Lambda}\times[0,t]) \) is a filtration.

label: eq:Trans-prob
title: Definition
body_md:
A \emph{transition matrix}\index{transition matrix}
\( \mathbf{P}(s, (r_{-1},r_{0},r_{1})) \)\gloprocp.cap@\( \mathbf{P}(s, (r_{-1},r_{0},r_{1})) \).)))
is a function \( \mathbf{P}:{\mathbb{S}}^{4}\to[0,1] \) with the property
 \( \sum_{s}\mathbf{P}(s,{\mathbf{r}})=1 \).
For an arbitrary history \( \eta \), and space-time point 
\( (x,t) \), denote
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:Trans-prob}
 \overline{\mathbf{P}}(\eta, s, x, t)
    = \mathbf{P}(s, (\eta(x-1,t),\eta(x,t),\eta(x+1,t))).
 \end{equation}
  We will omit the parameter \( \eta \) when it is clear from the context.

A \emph{probabilistic cellular automaton}\index{cellular
automaton!probabilistic} 
 \gloprocPCA@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{PCA\/}}}(\mathbf{P}, {\Lambda}) \).))) 
 \[
  \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{PCA\/}}}(\mathbf{P}, {\Lambda})
 \]
  is characterized by saying which random histories are
considered \emph{trajectories}\index{trajectory}.
Now a trajectory is not a single history (sample path)
but a distribution over histories that satisfies the
following condition, saying
that the random history \( \eta \) is a
trajectory if and only if the following holds.
Let \( s_{1},\dots, s_{n}\in{\mathbb{S}} \).
 \begin{equation*}
 \operatorname{\mathsf P}{\Bigl(\mskip 1mu\bigcap_{i=1}^{n}\{\eta(x_{i},t)=s_{i}\} \Bigm\vert \mathcal{A}_{t-1}\mskip 1mu\Bigr)}
 = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \overline{\mathbf{P}}(\eta, s_{i}, x_{i}, t-1).
 \end{equation*}
This expression uses the notion of conditional probability over sigma-algebras.
For a more elementary statement of the same property, 
let \( x_{0},\dots,x_{n+1} \) be given with \( x_{i+1}=x_{i}+1 \).
Let us fix an arbitrary history \( \zeta \) and an arbitrary
event \( \mathcal{H}\ni\zeta \) in \( \mathcal{A}_{t-1} \).
  Then we require
 \begin{multline*}
 \operatorname{\mathsf P}{\Bigl(\mskip 1mu\bigcap_{i=1}^{n}\{\eta(x_{i},t)=\zeta(x_{i},t)\} \cap
  \mathcal{H}\cap\bigcap_{i=0}^{n+1}\{\eta(x_{i},t-1)=\zeta(x_{i},t-1)\}\mskip 1mu\Bigr)}
 \\ =
 \operatorname{\mathsf P}{\Bigl(\mskip 1mu\mathcal{H}\cap\bigcap_{i=0}^{n+1}\{\eta(x_{i},t-1)=\zeta(x_{i},t-1)\}\mskip 1mu\Bigr)}
 \prod_{i=1}^{n} \overline{\mathbf{P}}(\eta, \zeta(x_{i},t), x_{i}, t-1).
 \end{multline*}
A probabilistic cellular automaton is \emph{noisy}\index{noisy} if
\( \mathbf{P}(s,{\mathbf{r}})>0 \) for all \( s,{\mathbf{r}} \).
Bandwidth can be defined for transition probabilities just as for
transition functions.
head: environment
name: Probabilistic cellular automaton

label: xmp:rand-gen
title: Example
body_md:
\label{xmp:rand-gen}
  As a simple example, consider a deterministic cellular automaton
with a ``random number generator''.
  Let the local state be a record with two fields, \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Det\/}}}} \)\gloprocdet@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Det\/}}}} \).)))
and \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Rand\/}}}} \) where \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Rand\/}}}} \)\gloprocrand@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Rand\/}}}} \).))) consists of a single bit.
  In a trajectory \( (\mu,\eta) \), the field \( \eta.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Det\/}}}}(x,t+1) \) is
computed by a deterministic transition function from \( \eta(x-1,t) \),
\( \eta(x,t) \), \( \eta(x+1,t) \), while \( \eta.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Rand\/}}}}(x,t+1) \) is obtained by
coin-tossing.

title: Definition
body_md:
Let us call a \emph{transition rate matrix} a function
\( \mathbf{R}:{\mathbb{S}}^{4}\to\left[0,\infty\right) \),\gloprocrem:cap@\( \mathbf{R}(s, {\mathbf{r}}) \).))) 
written as 
 \begin{align*}
 \mathbf{R}(s, {\mathbf{r}})\ge 0,
 \end{align*}
with the normalization property \( \mathbf{R}(r_{0}, \mathopen( r_{-1},r_{0},r_{1}\mathclose))=0 \) 
for all \( {\mathbf{r}} \).
Its elements are called the \emph{transition rates}\index{transition rate}.

label: eq:remember-field
title: Definition
body_md:
Suppose that the bit string that is a local state has some field \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}} \)
(it can for example be the first two bits of the state).
We will say that \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}} \) \emph{remembers}\index{remembering} field \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}} \)
over an infinite set of sites \( {\Lambda} \) if
there is an \( \varepsilon>0 \) such that for each string \( s\in\{0,1\}^{|\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}|} \) there
is a configuration \( \xi_{s} \) such that for all
trajectories \( (\mu,\eta) \) of the \( \varepsilon \)-perturbation
 \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}_{\varepsilon}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}, {\Lambda}) \) with \( \eta(\cdot,0)=\xi_{s} \), for all \( x,t \) we
 have
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:remember-field}
  \mu\mathopen\{\mskip 1mu\eta(x,t).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}\ne s\mskip 1mu\mathclose\}< f(t)+O(\varepsilon)\text{ where } \lim_{t\to\infty}f(t)=0.
\end{equation}
  We define similarly the notions of remembering a field for a
probabilistic transition matrix \( \mathbf{P} \) and a probabilistic
transition rate matrix \( \mathbf{R} \).

Let us call a configuration \( \xi \) \emph{homogeneous} if there is a state \( q\in{\mathbb{S}} \) such
that \( \xi(x)=q \) for all \( x \).
We say that \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}} \) remembers \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}} \) in a \emph{self-organizing way}
if the initial configurations \( \xi_{s} \) can be made homogeneous.
head: environment
name: Remembering some bits

label: thm:1dim.nonerg
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:1dim.nonerg}
  For any constant \( c_{1}>1 \) 
 there is a one-dimensional probabilistic transition matrix that remembers a field,
 in a self-organizing way;  the function \( f(t) \) in~\eqref{eq:remember-field}
can be chosen as \( t^{-c_{1}}\).
If the space is finite with size \( N \) then in any cell, at time \( t \),
the probability of forgetting it at time \( t \) is bounded by \( \varepsilon^{h_{0}(N,c_{2})} \)
for an appropriate constant \( c_{2} \).
head: environment
name: Remembering a field in discrete time

label: rem:sorg-poor
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:sorg-poor}
   The error term in~\eqref{eq:remember-field} improves with time, but 
   why does it not decrease with \( \varepsilon \)?
   Technically, in our proofs it is the price of the need for symmetry-breaking random
   choices in self-organization, but it still seems improvable.

body_md:

label: def:preceq
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:preceq}
Each field \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}} \) of a cell state such that the field size is even, can be
considered not only a binary string but a string of (half as many) symbols
in the standard alphabet.
  If \( r,s \) are strings in \( (\Sigma_{0})^{n} \) then 
 \gloproc"<@\( \preceq \).))) 
 \[
   r\preceq s
 \]
  will mean that \( s(i)=r(i) \) for all \( 0\le i<n \) such that \( r(i)\ne * \).
  For functions \( f, g \), with values in \( \Sigma_{0}^{*} \) we will write
\( f\preceq g \)  if for all \( s \) we have \( f(s)\preceq g(s) \).

name: Specification relation between strings

label: def:std-comp
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:std-comp}
Let \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}} \) be any deterministic
transition function with states in some alphabet \( \mathbb{A} \)
with distinguished fields \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Input\/}}}} \), \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Output\/}}}} \) in the standard alphabet.
We say that \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}} \) has \emph{monotonic output}\index{monotonic output} if
for all trajectories \( \eta \) of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}) \) we have
 \[
  \eta(x,t).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Output\/}}}} \preceq \eta(x,t+1).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Output\/}}}}.
\]
  We call the transition function \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}} \), all of whose fields have even
size (that is they are in the standard alphabet) together with some
distinguished fields \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Input\/}}}} \), \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Output\/}}}} \), a
\emph{standard computing transition function} if it
 \begin{cjenum} 

                                                                              

  \item never changes \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Input\/}}}} \);

  \item has monotonic output;

  \item does not change anything if
                                                
    the middle argument has all \( \# \)'s in its input field, or if all three
    arguments have \( * \) in all their fields.
    
 \end{cjenum}
We will call a cellular automaton with such a transition function a
\emph{standard computing medium}\index{medium!standard computing}.
Our construction uses for this a special field called 
\begin{align*}
 \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Color\/}}}}.
\end{align*}
It can take a constant number of values; in one case, only \( -1,0,1 \).
head: environment

label: def:Init
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:Init}
Let \( \Sigma_{0} \) be the standard input/output alphabet, and
\( {\mathbb{S}} \)  a set of states with \( {\mathbb{S}}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Input\/}}}}=\Sigma_{0} \),
having another field \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Color\/}}}}\in\{-1,0,1\} \), and
a distinguished ``latent'' state \( s_{0} \).
Let \( \psi_{*}:\Sigma_{0}^{*}\to{\mathbb{S}}^{*} \) be an encoding.
For any finite string \( \rho\in\Sigma_{0}^{n} \), let \( n'=|\psi_{*}(\rho)| \).
For any finite or infinite \( N>|\rho'| \), we construct the initial configuration
  \gloprocinit@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Init\/}}}_{\psi_{*}}(\rho) \).)))
	\begin{equation*}
      \xi'=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Init\/}}}_{\psi_{*}}(\rho)\in{\mathbb{S}}^{N}
    \end{equation*}
    as follows.
    Define \( \xi \) by setting
    \( \xi(x)=\psi_{*}(\rho)(x) \) for each \( x\in\left[0,n'\right) \), and \( s_{0} \)
    for all other \( x \).
    In case \( N=\infty \),  obtain \( \xi' \) from \( \xi \) by setting
    \begin{align*}
    \xi'(x).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Color\/}}}}=
      \begin{cases}
    0  & \text{ for } 0\le x<n, 
\\    -1 & \text{ for } x<0, 
\\    1 & \text{ for } x\ge n.
      \end{cases}
    \end{align*}
    When the space is the finite one \( \mathbb{Z}_{N} \) then, with \( r=(N-n)/2 \),
 set \( \xi'(x).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Color\/}}}}=-1 \) for \( -r\le x<0 \),  and \( 1 \) for \( n\le x < n+r \).
head: environment
name: Init

label: thm:1dim.comp
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:1dim.comp}
  Let \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}} \) be a standard computing transition function over an alphabet \( \Sigma \),
  and \( \delta>0 \) a constant.
  There is
 \begin{itemize}
  \item a transition function \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}' \) with a state space \( {\mathbb{S}} \) having fields \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Input\/}}}} \),
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Output\/}}}} \), \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Color\/}}}} \), with \( {\mathbb{S}}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Input\/}}}}={\mathbb{S}}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Output\/}}}}=\Sigma_{0} \).
\item a code \( \psi_{*}: \Sigma_{0}^{*}\to {\mathbb{S}}^{*} \), with  \( |\psi_{*}(\rho)|\le 2|\rho| \);
\item a constant \( c_{1}>1 \)   
 \end{itemize}
 such that the following holds for all \( \rho\in\Sigma_{0}^{*} \).
 Let \( \zeta(x,t) \) be any trajectory of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}} \) with
 \( \zeta(x,0).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Input\/}}}}=\rho(x) \) for \( x\in\left[0,|\rho|\right) \) and filled with \( * \)'s
 otherwise.
 Let \( \eta \) be any trajectory of an \( \varepsilon \)-perturbation of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}' \), with
 \( \eta(\cdot,0)=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Init\/}}}_{\psi_{*}}(\rho) \).
 For all \( t \), all \( t'> t\cdot h_{1}(t,c_{1}) \), all \( x\in\mathbb{Z} \) we have
 for all sufficiently small \( \varepsilon \):
 \[
 \operatorname{\mathsf P}\mathopen\{\mskip 1mu\zeta(x, t).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Output\/}}}} \not\preceq \eta(x, t').\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Output\/}}}}\mskip 1mu\mathclose\} <\delta.
\]
head: environment
name: Reliable computation in dim 1

label: rem:sorg-poorer
title: Remarks
body_md:
\label{rem:sorg-poorer}
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item 
  This note is similar to Remark~\ref{rem:sorg-poor}, but is even more important,
  as the error term does not even decrease with increasing \( t \).
\item The initialization via \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Init\/}}} \) avoids building up an infinite hierarchy in the
  initial configuration, leaving this to self-organization.
  But it introduces a huge asymmetry by coloring the left of the input with \( -1 \) and
  the right with \( 1 \).
  This has an effect similar to making the space infinite in only
  one direction, and placing the input into the beginning.
  \end{enumerate}

label: def:code
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:code}
  A code \( \varphi \)\gloprocf.greek@\( \varphi_{*},\varphi_{*} \).))) between two sets \( R,S \) is
a pair \( (\varphi^{*},\varphi_{*}) \) where \( \varphi_{*}: R\to S \) is the
\emph{encoding function} and \( \varphi^{*}: S\to R \) is the \emph{decoding function},
and the relation
 \[
  \varphi^{*}(\varphi_{*}(r)) = r
 \]
   holds.
We will be particularly interested in the example when 
for a positive integer \( {Q} \) called the \emph{block size} and some finite sets
\( {\mathbb{S}}_{1},{\mathbb{S}}_{2} \) we have \( R={\mathbb{S}}_{2} \),
\( S={\mathbb{S}}_{1}^{{Q}} \).
Such a code is called a \emph{block code}.
In a block code, strings of the form \( \varphi_{*}(r) \) are called \emph{codewords}.
The elements of a codeword \( s=\varphi_{*}(r) \) are numbered as
\( s(0),\dots,s({Q}-1) \).

The codes \( \varphi \) between sets \( R, S \) used in our simulations will have a
feature similar to the acceptance and rejection of 
Example~\ref{xmp:block-code}.
The set \( R \) will always have a subset of symbols called
\emph{vacant}\index{vacant symbols}, 
and among them a distinguished special symbol \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Vac\/}}} \)\gloprocvac@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Vac\/}}} \).))).
An element \( s\in S \) will be called
\emph{accepted}\index{accepted by decoding} by the decoding if
\( \varphi^{*}(s)\ne \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Vac\/}}} \), otherwise it is called \emph{rejected}.
head: environment
name: Code on strings

title: Remark
body_md:
The notation \( (\varphi^{*},\varphi_{*}) \) to use for decoding and encoding is not in
common use: I find it suggestive, though, since \( \varphi^{*} \) is something
like an inverse function without actually being one.

label: xmp:block-code
title: Example
body_md:
\label{xmp:block-code}
Suppose that \( {\mathbb{S}}_{1}={\mathbb{S}}_{2}=\{0,1\}^{12} \) is the state set of both
cellular automata \( M_{1} \) and \( M_{2} \).
Let us introduce the fields \( s.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Addr\/}}}} \) and
\( s.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Info\/}}}} \)\gloprocinfo@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Info\/}}}} \).))) of a state \( r=(s_{0},\dots, s_{11}) \) in
\( {\mathbb{S}}_{1} \).
The \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Addr\/}}}} \) field consists of the first 5 bits \( s_{0},\dots,s_{4} \),
while the \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Info\/}}}} \) field is the last bit \( s_{11} \).
The other bits do not belong to any named field.
Let \( {Q}=31 \).
Thus, we will use codewords of size \( 31 \), formed of the symbols (local
states) of \( M_{1} \), to encode local states of \( M_{2} \).
The encoding funcion \( \varphi_{*} \) assigns a codeword
\( \varphi_{*}(r)=(s(0),\dots, s(30)) \) of elements of \( {\mathbb{S}}_{1} \) to each
element \( r \) of \( {\mathbb{S}}_{2} \).
Let \( r=(r_{0},\dots, r_{11}) \).
We will set \( s(i).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Info\/}}}}=r_{i} \) for \( i=0,\dots,11 \).
The 5 bits in \( s(i).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Addr\/}}}} \) will denote the number \( i \) in binary
notation.
This did not determine all bits of the symbols \( s(0),\dots, s(30) \) in
the codeword.
In particular, the bits belonging to neither the \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Addr\/}}}} \) nor the
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Info\/}}}} \) field are not determined, and the values of the \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Info\/}}}} \) field
for the symbols \( s(i) \) with \( i\not\in\left[0,12\right) \) are not determined.
To determine \( \varphi_{*}(r) \) completely, we could set these bits to 0.

The decoding function is simpler.
Given a word \( s=(s(0),\dots,s(30)) \) we first check whether it is a
``normal'' codeword, and as such, 
has \( s(0).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Addr\/}}}}=0 \) and \( s(i).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Addr\/}}}}\ne 0 \) for \( i\ne 0 \).
If yes then \( r=\varphi^{*}(s) \) is defined by \( r_{i}=s(i).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Info\/}}}} \) for
\( i\in\left[0,12\right) \), and the word is accepted'.
Otherwise \( \varphi^{*}(s)=0\cdots 0 \), and the word is rejected.

Informally, the symbols of the codeword use their first 5 bits to mark
their address within the codeword.
The last bit is used to remember their part of the information about
the encoded symbol.
head: environment

label: xmp:code.aggreg
title: Example
body_md:
\label{xmp:code.aggreg}
The trivial example here will not be really used as a code but rather as a
notational convenience.
For every symbol set \( {\mathbb{S}}_{1} \), blocksize \( {Q} \) and \( {\mathbb{S}}_{2}={\mathbb{S}}_{1}^{{Q}} \),
there is a special block code \( \iota_{{Q}} \)\gloproci:greek@\( \iota_{{Q}} \).))) called
\emph{aggregation}\index{aggregation} defined by
 \[
  \iota_{{Q}}^{*}((s(0),\dots,s({Q}-1)))=s(0)\sqcup\cdots\sqcup s({Q}-1),
 \]
and \( \iota_{{Q}*} \) defined accordingly.
Thus, \( \iota_{{Q}}^{*} \) is essentially the identity: it just aggregates \( {Q} \)
symbols of \( {\mathbb{S}}_{1} \) into one symbol of \( {\mathbb{S}}_{2} \).
We use concatenation here since we identify all symbols with binary
strings.

\label{def:control}
 Assume that code \( \varphi \) aggregates field \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}_{1} \) into \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}_{2} \).
 We say that field \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}_{1} \) \emph{controls} address \( a \) for code \( \varphi \)

title: Definition
body_md:
A \emph{dwell period}\index{period!dwell} of \( \eta \)
is a tuple \( (x,s,t_{1},t_{2}) \)
such that \( x \) is a site, \( s \) is a nonvacant state, and \( 0\le t_{1}<t_{2} \)
are switching times with \( \eta(x,t_{1})=s \).
The rectangle \( \left[x,x+{B} \right)\times \left[t_{1},t_{2}\right) \) is the
\emph{space-time body}\index{body!space-time} of the dwell period.

title: Definition
body_md:
A configuration is a \emph{lattice
     configuration}\index{configuration!lattice} if all cells are at sites of
the form \( i{B}  \) for integers \( i \).
We can also talk about \emph{lattice histories}\index{history}: these have
space-time bodies of the form
 \[
   \left[i{B} ,(i+1){B} \right)\times\left[j{T} ,k{T} \right)
 \]
  for integers \( i,j<k \).

name: Lattice configuration

label: def:determ-ca-param
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:determ-ca-param}
A \emph{deterministic cellular automaton}\index{cellular
automaton!deterministic} 
 \gloprocca@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}, {B} , {T} , {\Lambda}) \).))) 
 \[
   \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}, {B} , {T} , {\Lambda})
 \]
 is determined by parameters 
\( {B} ,{T} >0 \) and a transition function \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}:{\mathbb{S}}^{3}\to{\mathbb{S}} \).
We may omit some obvious arguments from this notation.
A lattice history \( \eta \) with parameters \( {B} ,{T}  \) is a
\emph{trajectory}\index{trajectory!deterministic cellular automaton} of this
automaton if
 \[
   \eta(x,t)=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}(\eta(x-{B} ,t-{T} ), \eta(x,t-{T} ), \eta(x+{B} ,t-{T} ))
 \]
 holds for all \( x,t \) with \( t\ge {T}  \).
For a history \( \eta \) let us write 
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:trans-B}
   \overline{\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}}(\eta, x,t,{B} )=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}(\eta(x-{B} ,t), \eta(x,t), \eta(x+{B} ,t)).
 \end{equation}

name: Deterministic cellular automaton with size parameters

A medium is said to have a \emph{variable period}\index{medium!variable-period}
if in its histories, not all dwell periods have necessarily the same size.

name: Variable-period cellular medium

title: Definition
body_md:
A block code will be called
\emph{overlap-free}\index{code!block!overlap-free} if for every string
\( \mathopen( s(0),\dots s(n-1)\mathclose) \), and all \( i\le n-{Q}  \), if both
strings \( \mathopen( s(0),\dots,s({Q} -1)\mathclose) \)
and \( \mathopen( s(i+1),\dots,s(i+{Q} -1)\mathclose) \) are accepted then \( i\ge {Q}  \).

name: Overlap-free

label: eq:cand.colony
title: Definition
body_md:
Suppose that a configuration \( \xi \) of \( M_{2} \), which is a cellular medium
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{AMed\/}}}({Q} {B} ) \), is given.
Then we define the encoded configuration \( \xi_{*}=\varphi_{*}(\xi) \) of \( M_{1} \),
which is an \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{AMed\/}}}({B} ) \), by setting for each cell \( x \) of \( \xi \) and
 \( 0\le i < {Q}  \),
  \[
   \xi_{*}(x + i {B} )=\varphi_{*}(\xi(x))(i).
  \]
Suppose that a configuration \( \xi \) of \( M_{1} \) is given.
We define the decoded configuration
 \( \xi^{*}=\varphi^{*}(\xi) \) of \( M_{2} \) as follows:
for site \( x \), set \( \xi'(x)=\varphi^{*}(s) \) where
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:cand.colony}
   s = \mathopen( \xi(x), \xi(x + {B} ), \dots, \xi(x + ({Q}  - 1){B} )\mathclose).
 \end{equation}
We define \( \xi^{*}(x)=\xi'(x) \) if the latter is vacant or
there is no \( y \) closer than \( {Q} {B}  \) to \( x \)
with \( \xi'(y) \) non-vacant; otherwise \( \xi^{*} = \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Vac\/}}} \).

label: def:code-config
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:code-config}

head: environment
name: Code configuration

title: Definition
body_md:
Suppose that \( M_{1} \) and \( M_{2} \) are deterministic cellular automata
where \( M_{i}=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{i},{B} _{i},{T}_{i}) \), and \( \varphi \) is a block code with
 \[
  {B} _{1}={B} ,\qquad {B} _{2}={Q} {B} .
 \]
  The decoding function may be as simple as in Example~\ref{xmp:block-code}:
there is an \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Info\/}}}} \) track and once the colony is 
accepted the decoding function depends only on this part of the
information in it.

For each history \( \eta \) of \( M_{1} \), we define the history
\( \eta^{*}=\varphi^{*}(\eta) \) of \( M_{2} \) by setting
 \begin{equation}
  \eta^{*}(\cdot,t)=\varphi^{*}(\eta(\cdot,t)).
 \end{equation}
  We will say that the code \( \varphi \) is a
 \emph{simulation}\index{simulation!block code} if for each configuration
\( \xi \) of \( M_{2} \), for the (unique) trajectory \( \eta \) 
of \( M_{1} \), such that \( \eta(\cdot,0)=\varphi_{*}(\xi) \), the
history \( \eta^{*} \) is a trajectory of \( M_{2} \).
head: environment
name: Block simulation between deterministic cellular automata

title: Example
body_md:
Let us show one particular way in which the transition
function \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{1} \) can make the code \( \varphi \) a simulation.
  Assume that
 \[
  {T}_{1}={T} ,\ {T}_{2}={U} {T} 
 \]
  for some positive integer \( {U}  \) called the
 \emph{work period size}\index{period!work!size}.
Each cell of \( M_{1} \) will go through a period consisting of \( {U}  \) steps
in such a way that the \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Info\/}}}} \) field will be changed only in the last
step of this period.
The initial configuration \( \eta(\cdot,0)=\varphi_{*}(\xi) \) is chosen in
such a way that each cell is at the beginning of its work period.
By the nature of the code, in the initial configuration, cells of
\( M_{1} \) are grouped into colonies.

Once started from such an initial configuration, during each work
period, each colony, in cooperation with its two neighbor colonies,
computes the new configuration.
With the block code in Example~\ref{xmp:block-code}, this may happen
as follows.
Let us denote by \( r_{-1},r_{0},r_{1} \) the value in the first 12 bits of
the \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Info\/}}}} \) track in the left neighbor colony, in the colony itself
and in the right neighbor colony respectively.
First, \( r_{-1} \) and \( r_{1} \) are shipped into the middle colony.
Then, the middle colony computes \( s=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{2}(r_{-1},r_{0},r_{1}) \)
where \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{2} \) is the transition function or \( M_{2} \) and stores it on
a memory track.
(It may help understanding how this happens if we think of the
possibilities of using some mail, memory and workspace tracks.)
Then, in the last step, \( s \) will be copied onto the \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Info\/}}}} \) track.
head: environment

label: xmp:sim.aggreg
title: Example
body_md:
\label{xmp:sim.aggreg} 
Here is a trivial example of a block simulation which will be
applied, however, later in the paper.
Given a one-dimensional transition function \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}(x,y,z) \) with
state space \( {\mathbb{S}} \), we can define for all positive integers \( {Q}  \) an
\emph{aggregated} transition function\index{transition function!aggregated}
 \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}^{{Q} }(u,v,w) \)\gloproctr@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}^{{Q} }(u,v,w) \).))) as follows.
The state space of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}^{{Q} } \) is \( {\mathbb{S}}^{{Q} } \).
Let \( {\mathbf{r}}_{j}=\mathopen( r_{j}(0),\dots, r_{j}({Q} -1)\mathclose) \) for \( j=-1,0,1 \) be three
elements of \( {\mathbb{S}}^{{Q} } \).
Concatenate these three strings to get a string of length \( 3{Q}  \) and
apply the transition function \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}} \) to each group of three
consecutive symbols to obtain a string of length \( 3{Q}  - 2 \) (the end
symbols do not have both neighbors).
Repeat this \( {Q}  \) times to get a string of \( {Q}  \) symbols of \( {\mathbb{S}} \):
this is the value of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}^{{Q} }({\mathbf{r}}_{-1},{\mathbf{r}}_{0},{\mathbf{r}}_{1}) \),
defining an \emph{aggregated cellular automaton} \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}^{{Q}},{Q},{Q}) \) where
we used the notation in Definition~\ref{def:determ-ca-param}.

For \( M_{1}=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}({\mathbb{S}},\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}},{B} ,{T} ) \) and
\( M_{2}=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}({\mathbb{S}}^{{Q} },\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}^{{Q} },{Q} {B} ,{Q} {T} ) \), the aggregation code \( \iota_{{Q} } \)
defined in Example~\ref{xmp:code.aggreg} will be a block simulation of
\( M_{2} \) by \( M_{1} \) with a work period consisting of \( {U} ={Q}  \) steps.
If along with the transition function \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}} \), there were some fields
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}},\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{G\/}}}},\dots\subseteq\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{All\/}}}} \) also defined then we define, say, the field \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}} \) in
the aggregated cellular automaton as \( \bigcup_{i=0}^{{Q} -1}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}+i{\lVert {\mathbb{S}}\rVert}) \).
Thus, if \( {\mathbf{r}}=r(0)\sqcup\dotsm\sqcup r({Q} -1) \) is a state of the aggregated
cellular automaton then
 \( {\mathbf{r}}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}=r(0).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}\sqcup r(1).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}\sqcup\dotsm\sqcup r({Q} -1).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}} \).

We may allow only less communication
with the neighbors, and then modify the above as follows to a function
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}^{{Q},w } \) as follows, where we call \( \delta \) the \emph{slowdown rate}, where
we assume that \emph{both \( \delta{Q} \) and \( 1/\delta \) are integers}.
The state space is still \( {\mathbb{S}}^{{Q} } \).
Let \( {\mathbf{r}}_{j}=\mathopen( r_{j}(0),\dots, r_{j}({Q} -1)\mathclose) \) for \( j=-1,0,1 \) be three
elements of \( {\mathbb{S}}^{{Q} } \).
Concatenate these three strings to get a string of length \( 3{Q}  \) and
apply the transition function \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}} \) to each group of three
consecutive symbols to obtain a string of length \( 3{Q}  - 2 \) (the end
symbols do not have both neighbors).
Repeat this \emph{only \( w{Q}  \) times}
to get a string of \( {Q}  \) symbols of \( {\mathbb{S}} \):
this is the value of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}^{{Q},\delta }(r_{-1},r_{0},r_{1}) \).
This defines the cellular automaton \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}^{{Q},\delta},{Q},\delta{Q}) \).
The function \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}^{{Q}} \) becomes the special case \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}^{{Q},1} \).
Denoting by \( s.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{slice\/}}}}^{\delta,-1} \), \( s.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{slice\/}}}}^{\delta,1} \)
the leftmost and rightmost  \( \delta|{Q}| \) symbols of
a string \( s \) in \( {\mathbb{S}}^{{Q}} \),
then in fact \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}^{{Q},\delta}({\mathbf{r}}) \) depends only on
\( r_{-1}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{slice\/}}}}^{\delta,1},r_{0},r_{1}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{slice\/}}}}^{\delta,-1} \).

label: def:general-simulation
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:general-simulation}
A \emph{simulation}\index{simulation} of medium \( M_{2} \) by 
medium \( M_{1} \) having the same system \( \{\mathcal{A}_{t}\}_{t\ge 0} \) of \( \sigma \)-algebras 
is given by a pair
\gloprocf.greek.cap@\( \Phi^{*} \).)))
\begin{align}  \label{eq:Phi}
   \Phi=(\varphi, \Phi^{*})  
\end{align}
where \( \Phi^{*} \) is a mapping of the set of histories of
\( M_{1} \) into those of \( M_{2} \) (the decoding), \( \varphi_{*} \) is a mapping of
the set of configurations of \( M_{2} \) to the set of configurations of
\( M_{1} \) (the encoding for initialization).
We will assume to \( \varphi_{*} \) always belongs also a decoding function \( \varphi^{*} \),
so they form a code \( \varphi=(\varphi_{*},\varphi^{*}) \).
Denote 
 \[
  \eta^{*}=\Phi^{*}(\eta).
 \]
 We require that for each configuration \( \xi \) of \( M_{2} \), each
 trajectory of \( \eta \) of \( M_{1} \) with
 \( \eta(\cdot,0) = \varphi_{*}(\xi) \)
the decoded history\( \eta^{*} \) is a trajectory of \( M_{2} \)
with \( \eta^{*}(\cdot,0)=\xi \).
head: environment
name: General simulation

title: Definition
body_md:
A simulation will be called
\emph{non-anticipating} \index{simulation!non-anticipating} if
for each \( t \) the random function
\( \eta^{*}(\cdot,t) \) is measurable in the \( \sigma \)-algebra \( \mathcal{A}_{t} \)
(this says that it does not depend on the future).
Let \( \sigma \) be the shift on one-dimensional configurations and histories: that is
\( (\sigma\xi)(x)=\xi(x+1) \), \( (\sigma\eta)(x,t)=\eta(x+1,t) \).
A simulation \( (\varphi,\Phi^{*}) \) is called \emph{shift-invariant} if both \( \varphi \) and
\( \Phi^{*} \) commute with the shift.
It is called \emph{local}\index{simulation!local} 
if there is a finite space-time rectangle 
 \( V^{*}=I\times (u,0] \)\gloprocv.cap@\( V^{*} \).))) 
with \( u\ge 0 \) such that
\( \Phi^{*}(\eta)(w,t) \) depends only on \( \eta((w,t)+V^{*}) \).
A local simulation is both non-anticipating and shift-invariant.

All our simulations will be local, unless stated otherwise.
It follows from the non-anticipating property that 
\( \eta^{*}(\cdot,0) \) depends only on
\( \eta(\cdot,0) \), and therefore the simulation always defines a decoding
function 
 \begin{align*}
  \varphi^{*}
 \end{align*}
 on configurations (as already stipulated in Definition~\ref{def:general-simulation}). 
                                                                    
                                             
                             
                                         
             
If \( u=0 \) and so the configuration \( \eta^{*}(\cdot,t) \) depends only on
the configuration \( \eta(\cdot,t) \), then the simulation will be called
\emph{memoryless}\index{simulation!memoryless}.
head: environment
name: Local simulation

label: def:trickle-down-1
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:trickle-down-1}
Let \( \Phi=(\varphi,\Phi^{*}) \) be a simulation as in~\eqref{eq:Phi} whose encoding
\( \varphi_{*} \) is a block code with block size \( {Q}  \), between abstract cellular
media \( M_{k} \) (\( k=1,2 \)).
Let \( D_{k}>0 \) (\( k=1,2 \)) be some parameters, and \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}_{1} \) 
a field of the medium \( M_{1} \).
We say that \( \Phi \) has the
\emph{\( \varepsilon \)-trickle-down property}\index{error!trickle-down} 
of field \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}_{k+1} \) into field \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}_{1} \) with respect
to \( D_{1}, D_{2} \) if the following holds for every configuration
\( \xi \) of \( M_{2} \) and every trajectory \( (\mu,\eta) \) of \( M_{1} \) with
\( \eta(\cdot, 0)=\varphi_{*}(\xi) \).

Recall the notation \( \preceq \) in Definition~\ref{def:preceq}.
Let \( \eta^{1}=\eta \), \( \eta^{2}=\Phi^{*}(\eta) \).
Let \( x_{1},x_{2} \) be sites where \( x_{1} \)
has address \( a \) in the \( {Q}  \)-colony with base \( x_{2} \), let \( t_{0} \) be some
time.
For \( k=1,2 \) let \( \mathcal{E}_{k}(x) \) be the event that \( \eta^{k}(x,t) \)
is non-vacant and \( \eta^{k}(x,t).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}_{k} \)
does not change during \( (t_{0}-D_{k},t_{0}+D_{k}] \).
Let \( \mathcal{E}'_{1} \) be the event that \( \mathcal{E}_{1}(x_{1}) \) holds and also
 \[
   \eta(x_{1}, t).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}_{1} \succeq \varphi_{*}(\eta^{*}(x_{2}, t))(a).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}_{1}
 \]
 during this time.
Then \( \operatorname{\mathsf P}( \mathcal{E}_{2}(x_{2})\setminus\mathcal{E}')<\varepsilon \).
head: environment
name: Trickle-down

title: Definition
body_md:
A cellular medium \( M \) 
is called \emph{initially stable} for an initial configuration \( \xi \) 
with parameters \( (\varepsilon,{T} ) \)
if for each trajectory \( \eta \) of \( M \) with
\( \eta(\cdot,0)=\xi \), for each site \( x \), we have
 \[
  \operatorname{\mathsf P}\mathopen\{\mskip 1mu\cmexists\, t < {T} \;\eta(x,t) \ne \eta(x,0)\mskip 1mu\mathclose\} < \varepsilon.
 \]
head: environment
name: Initial stability

title: Example
body_md:
Consider the perturbation \( M=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}_{\varepsilon}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}},{B} ,{T} ) \)
of  a 1-dimensional deterministic cellular automaton.
Then for any configuration \( \xi \) and arbitrary \( \delta>0 \)
the medium \( M \) is initially stable for initial configuration \( \xi \) and parameters
\( (\delta,{T} ) \).
Indeed, by definition no cell is changing it state before time \( {T}  \).
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
If \( \varphi,\psi \) are two codes then \( \varphi\circ\psi \) is defined by
\( (\varphi\circ\psi)_{*}(\xi)=\varphi_{*}(\psi_{*}(\xi)) \) and
\( (\varphi\circ\psi)^{*}(\zeta)=\psi^{*}(\varphi^{*}(\zeta)) \).
It is assumed that \( \xi \) and \( \zeta \) are here configurations of the
appropriate cellular automata, that is the cell body sizes are in the
corresponding relation.
The code \( \varphi\circ\psi \)\gloproc"+@\( \circ \).))) is called the
\emph{composition}\index{code!composition} of \( \varphi \) and \( \psi \).
head: environment
name: Composition of codes

title: Example
body_md:
Let \( M_{1},M_{2},M_{3} \) have cell body sizes \( 1,31,31^{2} \)
respectively.
Let us use the code \( \varphi \) from Example~\ref{xmp:block-code}.
The code \( \varphi^{2}=\varphi\circ\varphi \) maps each cell \( c \) of \( M_{3} \) with body
size \( 31^{2} \) into a ``supercolony''\index{supercolony} of \( 31\cdot 31 \)
cells of body size 1 in \( M_{1} \).

Suppose that \( \zeta=\varphi_{*}^{2}(\xi) \) is a configuration obtained by
encoding from a lattice configuration of body size \( 31^{2} \) in \( M_{3} \),
where the bases of the cells are at positions \( -480 + 31^{2} i \).
(We chose -480 only since \( 480=(31^{2}-1)/2 \) but we could have chosen any
other number.)
Then \( \zeta \) can be grouped into colonies of size \( 31 \) starting at
any of those bases.
Cell 55 of \( M_{1} \) belongs to the colony with base \( 47=-480+17\cdot 31 \)
and has address 8 in it.
Therefore the address field of \( \zeta(55) \) contains a binary
representation of 8.
The last bit of this cell encodes the 8-th bit the of cell (with base)
47 of \( M_{2} \) represented by this colony.
If we read together all 12 bits represented by the \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Info\/}}}} \) fields of
the first 12 cells in this colony we get a state \( \zeta^{*}(47) \) (we count
from 0).
The cells with base \( -15+31j \) for \( j\in\mathbb{Z} \) with states
\( \zeta^{*}(-15+31j) \) obtained this way are also broken up into colonies.
In them, the first 5 bits of each state form the address and the
last bits of the first 12 cells, when put together, give back the
state of the cell represented by this colony.
Notice that these 12 bits were really drawn from \( 31^{2} \) cells of
\( M_{1} \).
Even the address bits in \( \zeta^{*}(47) \) come from different cells of
the colony with base 47.
Therefore the cell with state \( \zeta(55) \) does not contain information
allowing us to conclude that it is cell 55.
It only ``knows'' that it is the 8-th cell within its own colony
(with base 47) but does not know that its colony has address 17 within
its supercolony (with base \( -15\cdot 31 \)) since it has at most one
bit of that address.

label: def:xi^k
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:xi^k}
A \emph{hierarchical code}\index{code!hierarchical} is given by a sequence
 \gloprocf.greek.hier@\( \varphi_{k*} \).))) 
\( {\mathbb{S}}_{k},\varphi_{k*} \), (\( k\ge 1 \))
where \( {\mathbb{S}}_{k} \) is an alphabet and \( \varphi_{k*} \) is a code on configurations.
In the present work we will also assume that \( \varphi_{k*} \) always comes from a block
code 
 \begin{align*}
  \varphi_{k*}:{\mathbb{S}}_{k+1}\to{\mathbb{S}}_{k}^{{Q}_{k}}.
 \end{align*}
 \gloprocq.cap@\( {Q}_{k} \).))) 
Since \( {\mathbb{S}}_{k} \) and \( {Q}_{k} \) are implicitly defined by \( \varphi_{k*} \) we can
refer to the code as just \( (\varphi_{k*})_{k\ge 1} \).
  Consider a hierarchical code  \( (\varphi_{k*})_{k\ge 1} \) with state sequence \( ({\mathbb{S}}_{k}) \)
  and block sizes \( ({Q}_{k}) \).
  If for each \( {\mathbb{S}}_{k} \) a field \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}_{k} \) is also given, and
  the code \( \varphi_{k*} \) is aggregating from \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}_{k} \) to \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}_{k+1} \) as in
  Definition~\ref{def:aggreg-field}, then the hierarchical code \( (\varphi_{k*})_{k\ge 1} \)
  will be called \emph{aggregating} for the field sequence \( (\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}_{k}) \).
  If also \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}_{k} \) controls address 1 via a function \( \gamma_{k} \)
  (as by Definition~\ref{def:control}) then sequence of triples
  \begin{align}\label{eq:H}
   \mathbf{H} = (\varphi,\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}_{k}, \gamma_{k})_{k\ge 1}
  \end{align}
  will be called a \emph{centrally aggregating hierarchical code}, or shortly, a \emph{code complex}.

label: def:coord-hier
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:coord-hier}
Suppose that a code configuration \( \xi \) of a hierarchical code
\( (\varphi_{k})_{k\ge 1} \) with block sizes \( {Q}_{k} \) is given.
The sizes of the higher-order cells are defined by \gloprocb.cap@\( B_{k} \).))) 
\(  {B} _{1}= 1 \), \( {B} _{k+1} = Q_{k}{B}_{k} \).
For a finite or infinite \( n \), let \gloprock.cap@\( K_{0}(n) \).)))
\begin{align}\label{eq:K0}
 K_{0}(n) = \sup_{{B} _{k}\le n} k.
\end{align}
If \( n<\infty \)  then this is the largest \( k \) for which a \( k \)-cell can fit into \( \mathbb{Z}_{n} \).
As long as \( k< K_{0}(n) \)
the origin of our space \( {\Lambda} \) will be contained in some cell \( x_{k} \) of level \( k \).
Since it is in our power to define the code configuration \( \xi \), for simplicity
we will always arrange that \( x_{k} \) is the second cell (the cell with address 1)
of the colony coding cell \( x_{k+1} \).
In general, we could use any addresses \( 0<a_{k}<{Q}-1 \) instead of setting them always to 1,
but this is not important now.
Setting \( a_{k}=1 \) gives
\begin{align*}
  x_{1}=0, \quad  x_{k}  = -{B} _{1} - \cdots - {B} _{k-1} \text{ for } k>1.
\end{align*}

label: def:encoding-finite
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:encoding-finite}
  Given a code complex \( \mathbf{H} \) as above and
 a string \( \rho\in\Sigma_{0}^{n} \) we define its encoding
 \( \xi=\psi_{*}(\rho)\in{\mathbb{S}}^{\infty} \) which has the property that
 except for an interval of size \( \le 2 n \), \( \xi(x)=q_{{\mathbb{S}}} \) with
 \( q_{{\mathbb{S}}} \) as in Definition~\ref{def:Init}. 
  Let \( k=K_{0}(n) \) as in~\eqref{eq:K0}.
  Create the string 
\begin{align*}
 \rho'=*^{-x_{k}}\rho *^{l}
\end{align*}
where \( -x _{k} \) stars come at the front and the \( l \) stars at the back are the fewest
to make \( |\rho'|=m{B}_{k} \) an integer multiple of \( {B}_{k} \).
Now create a string \( r_{k}\in {\mathbb{S}}_{k}^{m} \) as follows.
First let \( r'_{k}=q_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{m} \), and then obtain \( r_{k} \) by replacing the track
\( r'_{k}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}_{k} \) in it with \( \rho' \).
Define the string \( r_{k-1}=\varphi_{i*}(r_{k})\in{\mathbb{S}}_{k-1}^{m{Q}_{k-1}} \).
Similarly, for each \( 1\le i<k \) let \( r_{i}=\varphi_{(i+1)*}(r_{i+1}) \).
By definition of the codes \( \varphi_{i*} \),
string \( r_{i} \) consists of \( m{Q}_{k-1}{Q}_{k-2}\cdots{Q}_{i} \) symbols of \( {\mathbb{S}}_{i} \).
Then \( r_{1} \) consists of \( m{B}_{k} \) symbols of \( {\mathbb{S}}={\mathbb{S}}_{1} \).
Finally obtain \( \xi \) as follows: \( \xi(x)=r(x-x_{k}) \) for \( 0\le x-x_{k}<m{B}_{k} \) and \( q_{{\mathbb{S}}} \)
otherwise.

label: def:amp
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:amp}
  Suppose that a sequence \( M_{1},M_{2},\dots \) of abstract media is given
along with simulations \( \Phi_{1},\Phi_{2},\dots \) such that \( \Phi_{k} \) is a
simulation of \( M_{k+1} \) by \( M_{k} \).
Such a system will be called an \emph{amplifier}\index{amplifier}.

label: def:amp-trickle
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:amp-trickle}
  Suppose that an amplifier \( \mathbf{\Psi}=(M_{k},\Phi_{k})_{k\ge 1} \) is given along
  with the sequences of parameters \( D_{k} \),
                          
  \( \varepsilon''_{k} \), \( \varepsilon_{k} \), and fields \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}_{k} \).
  Assume that each \( \varphi_{k} \) aggregates field \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}_{k} \) into \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}_{k+1} \),
  as in Definition~\ref{def:aggreg-field}.
 \begin{enumerate}

 \item \( \mathbf{\Psi} \) has the 
 \emph{trickle-down}\index{amplifier!trickle-down} property if for
 each \( k \), the simulation \( \Phi_{k} \) has the trickle-down
property of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}_{k+1} \) to \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}_{k} \) with                   
parameters  \( D_{k} \), \( D_{k+1} \) and \( \varepsilon''_{k} \),
as in Definition~\ref{def:trickle-down-1}.

 \item Suppose that the sequence \( \varepsilon_{k}>0 \), \( k=1,2,\dots \) is given 
with \( \sum_{k}\varepsilon_{k}<1/6 \), and also a configuration \( \xi \) of \( M_{1} \)
that is a code configuration of the code sequence \( (\varphi_{k}) \)
(as introduced in Definition~\ref{def:xi^k}).
We say that \( \mathbf{\Psi} \) has the \emph{initial stability property} with respect
to the initial configuration \( \xi \) and parameters \( ((\varepsilon_{k},{T}_{k}))_{k\ge 1} \)
if for each \( k \) the medium \( M_{k} \) has the initial stability
property for initial configuration \( \xi^{k} \) and parameters \( (\varepsilon_{k},2D_{k}) \).
 \end{enumerate}

label: def:err-code
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:err-code}
  A block code \( \varphi=(\varphi_{*}, \varphi^{*}) \) with \( \varphi^{*}: R^{{Q} }\to S \) will be called
  is \(  t \)-\emph{error-correcting} \index{code!error-correcting} 
  if for all \( x\in\Sigma \), \( y\in\Sigma^{\\Q } \) we
have \( \varphi^{*}(y)=x \) whenever \( y \) differs from
\( \varphi_{*}(x) \) in at most \( t \) symbols.
It is \( (\beta,t) \)-\emph{burst-error-correcting}
if for all \( x\in S \), \( y\in R^{\\Q } \) we
have \( \varphi^{*}(y)=x \) whenever \( y \) differs from
\( \varphi_{*}(x) \) in at most \( t \) intervals of size \( \le\beta \).
For such a code, we will say that a word \( y\in R^{\\Q } \) is \( (\beta, r) \)-\emph{compliant}
if it differs from a codeword of the code by at most \( r \) intervals of size \( \le\beta \).

Assume that strings \( R \) and \( S \) are in \( \{0,1\}^{*} \).
In the context of error-correcting codes, elements of \( R \) will be called the
\emph{symbols} of the codewords, as opposed to \emph{bits}, since each symbol may
consist of several bits.
head: environment
name: Error-correcting code

label: xmp:err-corr-code
title: Example
body_md:
\label{xmp:err-corr-code}
A popular kind of error-correcting code are codes \( \psi \) such that
\( \psi_{*} \) is a linear mapping when the binary strings in \( S \) and \( R^{{Q} } \)
are considered vectors over the field \( \{0,1\} \).
These codes are called \emph{linear codes}\index{code!linear}.
It is sufficient to consider linear codes \( \psi \) that are \emph{systematic}:
for all \( s \), the first \( {\lVert S\rVert} \) bits of the codeword \( \psi_{*}(s) \) are
identical to \( s \): they are called the
\emph{information bits}\index{code!bits!information}.
(If a linear code is not such, it can always be rearranged to have this
property.)
In this case, the remaining bits of the codeword are called
\emph{error-check bits}\index{code!bits!error check}, and they are linear
functions of \( s \).
For correcting a single error, in the tripling method outlined
in Section~\ref{sec:ftol-block}, the error check bits are simply the twice repeated
information bits.
head: environment

label: xmp:RS-code
title: Example
body_md:
\label{xmp:RS-code}\index{code!Reed-Solomon}
Here we define the linear code we will be using in later construction (a
generalization of the so-called Reed-Solomon code, see~\cite{Blahut83}).
In its application in our paper only its basic quantitative
properties are used, so the details can safely be skipped at first reading.

Let our codewords (information symbols and check symbols together) be
binary strings of length \( N l \)\gloprocn:cap@\( N \).)))\gloprocl@\( l \).))) for some \( l \),
\( N \).
The \emph{symbols} of our codewords, 
binary strings of length \( l \), will be interpreted as elements of the
finite field \( \mathrm{GF}(2^{l}) \)\index{Galois field}\gloprocgf@\( \mathrm{GF}(2^{l}) \).))) and
thus, each binary string \( c \) of length \( N l \) will be treated as a vector
\( \mathopen( c(0),\dots,c(N - 1)\mathclose) \) over \( \mathrm{GF}(2^{l}) \).
(Note that the word ``field'' is used in two different senses in the
present paper.)
Let us fix \( N \) distinct nonzero elements
\( \alpha_{i} \)\gloproca.greek@\( \alpha_{i} \).))) of \( \mathrm{GF}(2^{l}) \) and let \( t < N/2 \) be a
positive integer.
The codewords are those vectors \( c \) that satisfy the equations
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:RS-code}
  \sum_{i = 0}^{N - 1}\alpha_{i}^{j}c(i).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}^{k} = 0\ (j = 1,\dots, 2t)
 \end{equation}
where the addition, multiplication and taking to power \( j \) are
performed in the field \( \mathrm{GF}(2^{l}) \).
These are \( 2t \) linear equations.
If we fix the first \( N - 2t \) elements of the vector in any way, (these
are the \emph{information symbols}) the remaining \( 2t \) elements (the \emph{error check
symbols}) can be chosen in a way to satisfy the equations.
This set of equations is always solvable, since its determinant is a
Vandermonde determinant.

Below, we will show a procedure for correcting any \( \nu \le t \) nonzero
errors.
This demonstrates that for the correction of error in any \( \le t \) symbols,
only \( 2t \) error-check symbols are needed.
(Robert Solovay noticed that in our applications,
with a little deterioration of efficiency, even the most brute-force
decoding algorithm is sufficient.
We will never have to correct more than some constant number \( c \) of errors,
so the complexity of decoding would never go much over \( n^{c} \) steps.)

If \( E =\mathopen( e_{0},\dots, e_{N - 1}\mathclose) \) is the sequence of errors then \( C + E \)
will be the observed the word.
Only \( e_{i_{r }} \) are nonzero for \( r =1,\dots,\nu \).
Let \( Y_{r }=e_{i_{r }}, X_{r }=\alpha_{i_{r }} \).
We define the \emph{syndrome} \( S_{j} \) for \( j=1,\dots,2t \) by
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:S_{j}}
	S_{j} = \sum_{i} (c_{i}+e_{i})\alpha_{i}^{j}
		= \sum_{i} e_{i}\alpha_{i}^{j} 	
	   	= \sum_{r } Y_{r } X_{r }^{j}
 \end{equation}
  which can clearly be computed from the codeword: it is the amount by
which the codeword violates the \( j \)-th error check equation.
We will show, using the last expression, that \( Y_{r } \) and \( X_{r } \) can be
determined using \( S_{j} \).
Define the auxiliary polynomial
 \[
	\Lambda(x)=\prod_{r }(1-xX_{r })=\sum_{s=0}^{\nu} \Lambda_{s} x^{s}
 \]
 whose roots are \( X_{r }^{-1} \).
Let us show how to find the coefficients \( \Lambda_{s} \) for \( s>0 \).
We have, for any \( r = 1,\dots, \nu \), and any \( j = 1, \dots, 2t - \nu \):
 \[
	0	= Y_{r }X_{r }^{j+\nu}\Lambda(X_{r }^{-1})		
		= \sum_{s} \Lambda_{s} Y_{r } X_{r }^{j+\nu-s}.     
 \]
  Hence, summing for \( r  \), 
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:key}
	0 = \sum_{s = 0}^{\nu} \Lambda_{s}(\sum_{r } Y_{r } X_{r }^{j+\nu-s})
	= \sum_{s = 0}^{\nu} \Lambda_{s} S_{j+\nu-s}\ (j = 1,\dots, 2t - \nu)
 \end{equation}
  hence using \( \Lambda_{0}=1 \),
 \( \sum_{s=1}^{\nu} \Lambda_{s} S_{j+\nu-s}=-S_{j+\nu} \).
This is a system of linear equations for \( \Lambda_{s} \) whose coefficients are
the syndroms, known to us, and whose matrix \( M_{\nu} \) is nonsingular.
Indeed, \( M_{\nu} = ABA^{T} \) where \( B \) is the diagonal matrix
\( {\mathopen\langle Y_{r }X_{r }\mathclose\rangle} \) and \( A \) is the Vandermonde matrix \( A_{j,r }=X^{j-1}_{r } \).

A decoding algorithm now works as follows.
For \( \nu = 1,2,\dots,t \), see if \( M_{\nu} \) is nonsingular, then compute
\( \Lambda(x) \) and find its roots by simple trial-and-error, computing
\( \Lambda(\alpha_{i}^{-1}) \) for all \( i \).
Then, find \( Y_{r } \) by solving the set of equations~\eqref{eq:S_{j}} and
see if the resulting corrected vector \( C \) satisfies~\eqref{eq:RS-code}.
If yes, stop.
(There is also a faster way for determining \( \Lambda(x) \), via the Euclidean
algorithm, see~\cite{Blahut83}).

To make the code completely constructive we must find an effective
representation of the field operations of \( \mathrm{GF}(2^{l}) \).
This finite field can be efficiently represented as the set of remainders
with respect to an irreducible polynomial of degree \( l \) over \( \mathrm{GF}(2) \), so
what is needed is a way to generate large irreducible polynomials.
  Now, it follows from the theory of fields that
 \[
	x^{2\cdot 3^{s}} + x^{3^{s}} +1 
 \]
  is irreducible over \( \mathrm{GF}<(2) \) for any \( s \).
So, the scheme works for all \( l \) of the form \( 2\cdot 3^{s} \).

title: Remark
body_md:
The notion of ergodicity was defined only for trajectories of \( R_{\varepsilon} \)
that are also trajectories of some probabilistic cellular automaton \( R' \)
(as defined in Section~\ref{sec:PCA}) such that \( R'\subseteq R_{\varepsilon} \),
that is that all trajectories of \( R' \) are trajectories of \( R_{\varepsilon} \).
The difference between \( R_{\varepsilon} \) and \( R' \) is that the local
transition probabilities of a trajectory of \( R' \) are fixed and the
same everywhere in space-time, while \( R_{\varepsilon} \) requires them
only to be within some range.
Toom's theorem implies that no such \( R' \) is ergodic.

title: Example
body_md:
Let \( \xi_{0} \) be the configuration over the one-dimensional integer
lattice that is 0 in the even places and 1 in odd places, and \( \xi_{1} \)
the one that is 1 in the even places and 0 in the odd places.
For \( b=0,1 \) let \( \mu_{b} \) be the measure concentrated on \( \xi_{b} \),
and let \( P \) be the linear operator obtained from some transition function.
Suppose that the measures \( P^{n}\mu_{0} \) converge to some measure
\( \nu_{0} \).
Then the measures \( P^{n}\mu_{1} \) converge to some measure \( \nu_{1} \).
Even if \( \nu_{1} \) is different from \( \nu_{0} \) they differ only by a
translation in space.
If the translations of \( \nu_{0} \) are the only invariant measures of
\( P \) then we would still say that in some sense, \( P \) loses all
information about the initial configuration: we might say, it loses
all ``local'' information.
Indeed, a cell has no way of knowing whether it has even or odd
coordinates.

title: Definition
body_md:
Let us be given an arbitrary one-dimensional transition function
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}} \) and the integers \( N,L \).
We define the three-dimensional transition function \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}' \) as follows.
  The interaction neighborhood is \( H\times\{-1,0,1\} \) with the
neighborhood \( H \) defined in Section~\ref{sec:toom} above.
  The transition function \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}' \) says: in order to obtain your state at
time \( t+1 \), first apply the transition function \( R \) in each plane defined by
fixing the third coordinate.
  Then, apply transition function \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}} \) on each line obtained by fixing
the first and second coordinates.
\footnote{The papers~\cite{GacsReif3dim88} and \cite{Gacs2dim89} use a
neighborhood instead of \( H \) that makes some proofs easier: the
northern, south-eastern and south-western neighbors.}

For an integer \( m \), define the space \( {\Lambda} =\mathbb{Z}_{m}^{2}\times \mathbb{Z}_{N} \).
For a trajectory \( \xi \) of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}) \) on \( \mathbb{Z}_{N} \), define the
trajectory \( \zeta \) of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}') \) on \( {\Lambda} \) by
 \begin{equation} \label{eq:reifCode} 
	\zeta(i,j,n,t)=\xi(n,t).
 \end{equation} 
  Thus, each cell of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}) \) is repeated \( m^{2} \) times, on a whole
``plane'' (a torus for finite \( m \)) in \( {\Lambda} \).

title: Proposition
body_md:
There are constants
\( \varepsilon_{0},c_{1},d_{1}>0 \) such that the following holds.
For all \( N,L \), and \( m=c_{1} \log(N L) \), for any trajectory \( \xi \) of
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}) \) over \( \mathbb{Z}_{N} \), if the trajectory \( \zeta \) of
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}') \) is defined by~\eqref{eq:reifCode} then for any
\( \varepsilon<\varepsilon_{0} \), any trajectory \( (\mu,\eta) \) of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}_{\varepsilon}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}') \)
such that \( \eta(\cdot,0)=\zeta(\cdot,0) \) we have for all \( t \) in
\( (0,L] \) and all \( w\in {\Lambda} \)
 \[ 
  \mu\mathopen\{\mskip 1mu\eta(w,t)\ne  \zeta(w,t)\mskip 1mu\mathclose\} \le d_{1}\varepsilon .
 \]

label: thm:1dim.comp.finite
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:1dim.comp.finite}
  Let \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}} \) be a standard computing transition function over an alphabet \( \Sigma \),
  and \( \delta>0 \) a constant.
  There is
 \begin{itemize}
  \item a transition function \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}' \) with a state space \( {\mathbb{S}} \) having fields \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Input\/}}}} \),
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Output\/}}}} \);
\item a code \( \psi_{*}: \Sigma_{0}^{*}\to {\mathbb{S}}^{*} \) with \( |\psi_{*}(\rho)|\le 2|\rho| \),
  \item constants \( c_{1}, c_{2}>1 \)
 \end{itemize}
 such that the following holds for all sufficiently small \( \varepsilon \).
 Let \( N \) be the size of our space, and \( \rho\in\Sigma_{0}^{*} \) with
 \( 2|\rho|<N \), \( \varepsilon<\varepsilon_{0} \).
 Let \( \zeta(x,t) \) be any trajectory of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}} \) with
 \( \zeta(x,0).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Input\/}}}}=\rho(x) \) for \( x\in\left[0,|\rho|\right) \) and filled with \( * \)'s
 otherwise.
 Let \( \eta \) be any trajectory over the space \( \mathbb{Z}^{N} \)
 of an \( \varepsilon \)-perturbation of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}' \), with
 \( \eta(\cdot,0)=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Init\/}}}_{\psi_{*}}(\rho) \).
 For all sufficiently small \( \varepsilon \), for all
 \( t \) for which \( \zeta(\cdot,t) \) does not use more space than \( N \),
all \( t'>t\cdot h_{1}(t,c_{1}) \), all \( x\in\mathbb{Z} \) we have
 \[
 \operatorname{\mathsf P}\mathopen\{\mskip 1mu\zeta(x, t).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Output\/}}}} \not\preceq \eta(x, t').\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Output\/}}}}\mskip 1mu\mathclose\} < \delta + t'\varepsilon^{h_{0}(N,c_{2})}.
\]

label: xmp:PCA-medium
title: Example
body_md:
\label{xmp:PCA-medium}
\begin{sloppypar}
 Let us be given a probabilistic cellular automaton
$\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{PCA\/}}}(\mathbf{P},{B} ,{T} )$.
For each state vector ${\mathbf{r}}\in {\mathbb{S}}^{3}$ and state $s$, let us form type
$\alpha(s,{\mathbf{r}})$.                               
The condition of this type will say that the transition rules are obeyed at times
of the form $n{T} $.
Namely for cell $x$, time $t$ of the form $n{T} $ with $n>0$, let 
\end{sloppypar}
 \begin{align}\label{eq:PCA-medium}
\nonumber      {g}\bigl(\alpha(s,{\mathbf{r}}),\;\{x\} &\times(t-{T} ,t],\;\eta\bigr)
\\        &= \{ \eta(x+i{B} ,t-{T} /2)=r_{i}\;(i=-1,0,1),\;\eta(x,t)=s \},
\\    b(\alpha(s,r)) &= \mathbf{P}(s,{\mathbf{r}}).
 \end{align}
  For all cells $x$ and rational times $u$ we define a new type
 $\beta=\beta(x,u)$                        
 by $b(\beta(x,u)) = 0$ and
 \[
  {g}{\bigl(\mskip 1mu\beta(x,u),\;\{x\}\times[{T} {\lfloor u/{T} \rfloor},u],\;\eta\mskip 1mu\bigr)}
   = \mathopen\{\mskip 1mu\eta(x,u)\ne\eta(x,{T} {\lfloor u/{T} \rfloor})\mskip 1mu\mathclose\}.
 \]
This condition says that $\eta(x,u)=\eta(x,{T} {\lfloor u/{T} \rfloor})$ with probability 1.
For all other combinations $\alpha,V$ we set ${g}(\alpha,V,\eta)=0$.
It is easy to see that the trajectories of $\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{PCA\/}}}(\mathbf{P},{B} ,{T} )$ are
trajectories of the medium defined this way.

label: def:state-subsets
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:state-subsets}
In a probabilistic cellular automaton $\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{PCA\/}}}(\mathbf{P},{B} ,{T} )$ 
for each set of states $E$ and state vector ${\mathbf{r}}=(r_{-1},r_{0},r_{1})$ let
\( \mathbf{P}(E,{\mathbf{r}})=\sum_{q\in E}\mathbf{P}(q,{\mathbf{r}}) \).
Let $\mathbf{K}$\gloprock.cap@$\mathbf{K}$.))) be the set of functions $K:{\mathbb{S}}^{3}\to 2^{{\mathbb{S}}}$
such that
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:K-def}
  K({\mathbf{r}})\subseteq \mathopen\{\verythinmathskips\ne r_{0}: \mathbf{P}(s,{\mathbf{r}})>0\mskip 1mu\mathclose\}.
  \end{equation}
  For a space-time trajectory \( \eta \) and a \( K\in\mathbf{K} \) let us write 
 \gloprock.cap@\( \overline{K}(x,t,\eta) \).))) 
 \[
   \overline{K}(x,t,\eta)=K(\eta(x-{B} ,t), \eta(x,t), \eta(x+{B} ,t)).
 \]
  For all \( K',K''\in\mathbf{K} \) with \( K'\supseteq K'' \) (that is \( K'({\mathbf{r}})\supseteq K''({\mathbf{r}}) \)
  for all \( {\mathbf{r}} \)), let 
 \gloprocc.cap@\( c(K',K'') \).))) 
 \[
   c(K',K'') =\bigvee_{{\mathbf{r}}} \frac{\mathbf{P}(K''({\mathbf{r}}),{\mathbf{r}})}{\mathbf{P}(K'({\mathbf{r}}),{\mathbf{r}})}
 \]
  be the maximum conditional probability, over all \( {\mathbf{r}} \), of
getting into the set \( K''({\mathbf{r}}) \) provided we get into the set \( K'({\mathbf{r}}) \).  

In case of a continuous-time cellular automaton \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CCA\/}}}(\mathbf{R},{B} ) \),
for any functions \( K,K',K''\in\mathbf{K} \) with \( \mathbf{R}(K,{\mathbf{r}}) = \sum_{q\in K}\mathbf{R}(q,{\mathbf{r}}) \)
we define the corresponding quantity \gloprocc@\( c(K',K'') \).)))  
 \begin{align*}
c(K',K'')   = \bigvee_{{\mathbf{r}}}\frac{\mathbf{R}(K''({\mathbf{r}}),{\mathbf{r}})}{\mathbf{R}(K'({\mathbf{r}}),{\mathbf{r}})}.
 \end{align*}

title: Example
body_md:
Let \( M_{1}\) be the \( \varepsilon \)-perturbation \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}_{\varepsilon}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}},{B}_{1},{T}_{1}) \)
  of the cellular automaton with \( {\mathbb{S}}_{1}=\{0,1\} \) and
the trivial transition function  \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}(x,y,z)=0 \) for all \( x,y,z \).
Then \( \eta \) is a trajectory if for \( t>0 \), \( \eta(x,t) \) are 
random variables such that for any \( u \) and any finite set \( S \) of space-time points \( (x,t) \)
with \( t\ge u \), the conditional probability that
\( \eta(x,t)=1 \) in all \( (x,t)\in S \) no matter how the \( \eta(x',t') \) are fixed for all \( t'<t \),
is bounded by \( \varepsilon^{|S|} \).
The set of constraint types consists of a single element, \( \mathbb{T}_{1}=\{\alpha_{1} \} \)
with \( b_{1}(\alpha_{1})=\varepsilon \).
For the event function we have \( g_{1}(\alpha_{1},V,\eta)=1 \) if and only if
for some \( (x,t) \) of the form \( (m{B}_{1}, n{T}_{1}) \) with integers \( m,n \) and \( n>0 \),
\( V=\left[x,x+{B}_{1}\right)\times(t-T_{1},t] \), and \( \eta(x,t)=1 \).

Let  \( M_{2}\)  be  a medium with \( {\mathbb{S}}_{2}=\{0,1\} \).
For integers \( {Q}_{1},{U}_{1}>0 \) let \( {B}_{2}={Q}_{1}{B}_{1} \), \( {T}_{2}={U}_{1}{T}_{1} \).
The histories will be of the form \( \eta(x,t) \) with \( x=m{B}_{2} \), \( t=n{T}_{2} \) for \( n\ge 0 \).
The set of constraint types consists of a single element, \( \mathbb{T}_{2}=\{\alpha_{2} \} \)
with \( b_{2}(\alpha_{2})=3{Q}_{1}{U}_{1}\varepsilon^{2} \).
For the event function we have \( g_{2}(\alpha_{2},V,\eta)=1 \)
if and only if for some \( (x,t) \) of the form \( (n{B}_{1}, n{T}_{1}) \)
with integers \( m,n \) and \( n>0 \),
\( V=\left[x-{B}_{2},x+2{B}_{2}\right)\times(t-2{T}_{2},t] \),
and \( \eta(x,t)=1 \).

Let us define the simulation \( \varphi^{*} \) as follows.
If \( \eta^{*}=\varphi^{*}(\eta) \) then \( \eta^{*}(x,t)=1 \) if and only if
\( (x,t) \) has the form \( (m{B}_{2}, n{T}_{2}) \) with integers \( m,n \) and \( n>0 \),
and in \( V=\left[x-{B}_{2},x+2{B}_{2}\right)\times(t-2{T}_{2},t] \)
there are at least two elements \( (x_{1},t_{1})\ne (x_{2},t_{2}) \)  with \( \eta(x_{i},t_{i})=1 \).
To show that this is a simulation we define the system of local conditions
\[
   {\bigl(\mskip 1mu\beta_{i,j}(\alpha_{2},V), W_{i,j}(\alpha,V)\mskip 1mu\bigr)}
 \]
 as follows.
 These are nonempty if and only if for some \( (x,t) \)
 of the form \( (m{B}_{2}, n{T}_{2}) \) with integer \( m,n \) and \( n>0 \),
 \( V=\left[x-{B}_{2},x+2{B}_{2}\right)\times(t-2{T}_{2},t] \).
 In this case, let \( P=\{p_{1},\dots,p_{N}\} \) be a list of all distinct
 pairs \( \{ (x_{1},t_{1}), (x_{2},t_{2})\} \) in \( V \), where \( N=\binom{6{Q}_{1}{U}_{1}}{2} \).
 For \( p_{i}=\{ (x_{i,1},t_{i,1}), (x_{i,2},t_{i,2})\} \),
 let \( \beta_{i,j}(\alpha_{2},V)=\alpha_{1} \) for all \( i,j \),  and 
\begin{align*}
 W_{i,j}(\alpha_{2},V)=\left[x_{i,j},x_{i,j}+{B}_{1}\right)\times(t_{i,j}-{T}_{1},{T}_{i,j}].
\end{align*}
Then \( {g}_{2}(\alpha_{2},V,\eta^{*}) \) is the event that 
\( \eta(x,t)=1 \) for at least two pairs \( (x,t)\in V \),
and this is upper-bounded by 
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{i}\prod_{j}g_{1}(\alpha_{1},W_{i,j}(\alpha_{2},V))
\end{align*}
as required.
Also 
\begin{align*}
 b_{2}(\alpha_{2})=3{Q}_{1}{U}_{1}\varepsilon^{2}>N\varepsilon^{2}
=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\prod_{j=1}^{2}g_{1}(\alpha_{1},W_{i,j}(\alpha_{2},V))
\end{align*}
as required.
