body_md:
et \( I=(x_{0}-{B},x_{0}+{B}] \), then a cell's body intersects \( K \)
  if and only if it is in \( I \).
  Let \( t\in(t_{1},t_{2}] \).
  Suppose that \( K \) is controlled for all \( t'<t \),
  that is for all \( t'<t \),  each set \( I\times (t'-({p}_{0}+2)T^{\bullet},t'] \) contains some cell.
 Let \( t_{0}=t-({p}_{0}+2)T^{\bullet} \).
  We want to show that
  \begin{cjenum}
  \item\label{i:color-control.1}
    \( I \) contains some cell \( z \) at  some time in \( (t_{0},t] \),
  \item\label{i:color-control.2}
    at each such time the interval \( \Gamma(K,2{B}) \) intersects a cell body.    
  \end{cjenum}
  The statement~\ref{i:color-control.1}
  may not hold only if a cell \( x_{1} \) in \( I \)
  disappears at time \( t_{0} \), so assume this happens.
  Then \( x_{1} \) must have been erased by 
  some cell \( y_{1} \) about to create an adjacent neighbor whose body
  overlaps with the body of \( x_{1} \).
  Without loss of generality assume
\begin{align}\label{eq:lasting-control-0}
  x_{1}\le x_{0},\quad  y_{1}+{B}< x_{1}<y_{1}+2{B}.
\end{align}
As \( x_{1}>x_{0}-{B} \), we have 
\begin{align}\label{eq:lasting-control-1}
  x_{0}-3{B}<y_{1}<x_{1}-{B}\le x_{0}-{B} .
\end{align}
If \( y_{1}\in  I \) then let \( z\gets y_{1} \), now assume it is not.
According to the rule \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Adapt\/}}}} \), cell \( y_{1} \) must have had \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Dying\/}}}}_{0}=0 \),
  \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Creating\/}}}}_{1}=1 \) to be able to erase,
  and therefore survives until time \( t_{0}+{p}_{1}{T_{\bullet}} \) as \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Die\/}}}}({p}) \)
  always has \( {p}\ge{p}_{1} \) by Condition~\ref{cond:anim,kill}.
  Since according to Condition~\ref{cond:anim,kill} only the rule
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Create\/}}}} \) changes \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Creating\/}}}}_{1} \), and only when a right adjacent neighbor has
disappeared, cell \( y_{1} \) keeps trying to create a right neighbor.

\begin{step+}{step:lasting-control.success}
Suppose \( y_{1} \) succeeds in creating \( y_{1}+{B} \) before time \( t_{0}+2T^{\bullet} \).
\end{step+}
\begin{prooof}
  If \( y_{1}+{B}>x_{0}-{B} \) then set \( z\gets y_{1}+{B} \).
  Suppose \( y_{1}+{B}\le x_{0}-{B} \).
  Then \( y_{1}+{B} \) turns on \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Creating\/}}}}_{1} \) within time \( {p}_{0}T^{\bullet} \),
  and then tries to create \( y_{1}+2{B} \).
  If it succeeds then, by~\eqref{eq:lasting-control-1} we can set \( z\gets y_{1}+2{B} \).
  If it fails then a cell \( x_{2} \) with \( y_{1}+2{B}<x_{2}<y_{1}+3{B} \) is in the way,
  and we can set \( z\gets x_{2} \).
\end{prooof}                               

\begin{step+}{step:lasting-control.failure}
  Suppose that \( y_{1} \) does not succeed creating \( y_{1}+{B} \) before time \( t_{0}+2T^{\bullet} \).
\end{step+}
\begin{prooof}
  Then some cell \( x_{2} \) with  \( y_{1}+{B}<x_{2}<y_{1}+2{B} \) interferes.
  This cell was not there at time \( t_{0} \) as, by~\eqref{eq:lasting-control-0}, it
  would have overlapped with cell \( x_{1} \).
  Being so close to \( y_{1} \), cell \( x_{2} \) could not have
  arisen by spontaneous birth, hence it must have been created by \( x_{2}+{B} \)
  which, as any creating cell,  must still be alive after the creating time,
  so we can set \( z\gets x_{2}+{B} \).
\end{prooof}                               
We have shown~\ref{i:color-control.1}.
The proof also shows that unless \( x_{1} \) survives \( y_{1} \) will, therefore for all
\( t' \) in \( (t_{0},t] \), it is within \( 2{B} \) of interval \( K \), which
also shows~\ref{i:color-control.2}.

body_md:
\label{lem:germ-unexposed-later}
Consider a trajectory \( \eta \)
with a germ cell \( c_{1}=(x_{1},t_{1}) \), \( K=\left[x_{1},x_{1}+2{B}^{*}\right) \)
and \( L=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{G-size\/}}}}(c_{1}) \),
and assume that the large space-time rectangle~\eqref{eq:large-rect} is free of damage.
Let \( 5\tau_{2}R L\le H\le T^{\bullet *} \).
Then at some time \( t'\in[t_{1},t_{1}+H] \) we can find a cell \( x' \)
with a domain of germ size \( L'\ge L \), where
  \begin{align}\label{eq:germ-unexposed-later}
    x' \in \Gamma(x_{1},5 L'{B}).
\end{align}
If \( c'=(x',t') \) does not belong to an extended colony or to a  germ with maximal size
then \( t'=t_{1}+H \).
If \( L'\le\rho L \) then \( c'=c_{1} \), and during \( [t_{1},t_{1}+H] \)
the germ of \( c_{1} \) did not become exposed or have a neighbor that is a colony cell or
a germ cell with \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{G-size\/}}}}\ge\rho L \).

label: eq:H_i
title: Proof
body_md:
{step+}{step:birth.constr}
The following construction iterates that of Lemma~\ref{lem:germ-unexposed-later},
with cells \( c_{s}=(x_{s},t_{s}) \), \( L_{s}=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{G-size\/}}}}(c_{s}) \) and
time period of size
\begin{align}\label{eq:H_i}
  H_{s} = 10\lambda\tau_{2}R L_{s}
\end{align}
in step \( s \).
 \end{step+}
 \begin{prooof}
Starting with cell \( c_{1} \),
find a cell \( c' \) given by the conclusion of Lemma~\ref{lem:germ-unexposed-later},
call it \( c_{2}=(x_{2},t_{2}) \).
Repeat, getting to cells \( c_{3},c_{4},\dots \),
until cell \( c_{n} \) when
we reach a germ with maximal size, or a colony, or time \( t_{1}+2T^{\bullet *} \).
Let us call step \( s \) a \emph{growth step} if \( L_{s+1}\ge \rho L_{s} \), and
\emph{stalling step} otherwise.
As seen in Lemma~\ref{lem:germ-unexposed-later}, in a stalling step
a germ of \( c_{s} \) of size \( L_{s} \) does not get exposed, nor does it meet a
colony cell or a cell with \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{G-size\/}}}}\ge\rho L_{s} \).

Let us examine a stalling step  starting at time \( t_{s} \),
at the shorter end of the germ \( G_{s} \) of cell \( c_{s} \), that is
on the end in which direction its \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Grow-dir\/}}}} \) points; without loss
of generality, assume that it is the left end.
Let \( x_{s} \) be the cell of \( G_{s} \) with address \( {Q}/2 \).
After \( t_{s} \), the germ \( G_{s} \) may grow, but since it will not reach \( \rho L_{s} \),
it will stall soon, at some time \( u_{1} \).
One possibility is that the left end has reached its farthest possible address,
another that another germ is in the way: one with \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{G-size\/}}}} \) between \( L_{s}/\rho \)
and \( \rho L_{s} \); we already excluded the other possibilities.
In case the left end has reached the farthest address,
we will turn attention to the right end, so
without loss of generality, assume that the left end does not reach the farthest address,
because another germ \( G' \) is in the way.

Let \( x' \) be the central cell of \( G' \), and
look at the next \( \lambda+2 \) times in which \( x_{s} \) or \( x' \) make
a random choice of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Dominant\/}}}} \).
Let \( \mathcal{E} \) be the event that 
each choice is \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Dominant\/}}}}(x_{s})=1 \) and \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Dominant\/}}}}(x')=0 \).
We claim that if \( \mathcal{E} \) occurs then 
\( G_{s} \) will advance, so the current step is not a stalling step.
To avoid some case distinctions, call \( x_{s}=y_{1} \), \( x'=y_{0} \).
Let \( j \) be such that the first choice of
\( y_{1-j} \), at some time \( \tau \),  falls between two choices of \( y_{j} \)
at times \( \tau' \) and \( \tau'' \).
If \( \tau \) happens at least \( 0.1R L \) age steps before \( \tau'' \)
them \( G_{s} \) will advance before \( \tau'' \).
Otherwise \( G_{s} \) will advance soon after \( \tau'' \).
Now, \( \tau \) occurs before \( \lambda+1 \) choices made by \( y_{j} \);
indeed, \( T^{\bullet}/{T_{\bullet}}\le\lambda \) implies that the stages of \( y_{1-j} \) are at most
\( \lambda \) times longer than those of \( y_{j} \).
So the current step is stalling only if \( \neg\mathcal{E} \) holds, that is with probability
\begin{align*}
  \operatorname{\mathsf P}(\neg\mathcal{E}) \le 1-(1/2-\varepsilon')^{\lambda+2}< 1-(1/2-\varepsilon')^{5}<1-2^{-5},
\end{align*}
because \( \lambda\le 2 \) according to~\eqref{eq:lg-less-2}, and \( \varepsilon' \) can
be chosen small.

by Condition~\ref{cond:comput}\ref{i:comput.rand} on robust media.
 \end{prooof}                    

 \begin{step+}{step:birth.probab-estim}
   Let us estimate first the probability that there is no colony in~\eqref{eq:large-rect}
   informally (that is not in the sense of canonical simulation  yet).
 \end{step+}
 \begin{prooof}
   We assumed that the rectangle~\eqref{eq:large-rect} is damage-free; the straightforward
   estimation of the probability of damage will come later.
   Our construction gives in step \( s \) a cell \( c_{s}=(x_{s},t_{s}) \).
The number of growth steps is at most \( \log(5{Q})/\log\rho \).
Recalling~\eqref{eq:germ-signif-larger}, this is \( < 4\log{Q} \) when \( {Q} \) is large.
As \( L_{s}<5{Q} \), each  step  has time length \( \le 50\lambda\tau_{2}{Q} \).
So the total number of steps is at least
\begin{align}\label{eq:n-lb-1}
   n\geT^{\bullet *}/25\lambda{p}_{2}T^{\bullet}{Q}.
\end{align}
We are using the parameters in~\eqref{eq:amp-fr}:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:frame-values}
  \begin{aligned}
  {Q} &={Q}_{k}= R^{k+1},
\\ w &=1/R k^{2},
  \\ {U}' &= R{Q}/w,
  \\ T^{\bullet *} &< 2{U}'_{k}T^{\bullet} < 2T^{\bullet *},
  \\      \log{Q} &= (k+1)\logR.
  \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
so by~\eqref{eq:n-lb-1} we have
\begin{align}
\nonumber  T^{\bullet *}/{Q}T^{\bullet} &>{U}'/{Q}=R/w=R^{2}k^{2},
  \\\label{eq:n-lb}
  n &\ge R^{2}k^{2}/25\lambda{p}_{2}=:cR^{2}k^{2}.
\end{align}
 As we have seen the probability for any particular step \( s \) to be a stalling step is 
\( \le 1-2^{-5} \).
Using \( \ln (1+x)<1+x \) we have \( \ln (1-2^{-5})\le -2^{-5} \),
\begin{align}\label{eq:log-r}
   r := -\ln (1-2^{-5}) > 2^{-5}.
\end{align}
For any particular \( m \)-element subset of steps the probability to be stalling steps
is at most \( (1-2^{-5})^{m}=e^{-r m} \).
As seen, the number of stalling steps is at least \( n-4\log{Q} \),
so the probability of no colony is 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:prob-bd}
  \begin{aligned}
  &\le\sum_{i>n-4\log{Q}}\binom{n}{n-i}e^{-r(n-i)}
    = \sum_{i<4\log{Q}}\binom{n}{i}e^{-r(n-i)}
  \\ &<   4\log{Q} \cdot n^{4\log{Q}}e^{-r(n-4\log{Q})}
       = 4\log{Q} e^{-(rn-4r\log{Q}+4\ln n \log {Q})},    
  \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
because the term inside the sum is increasing with \( i \).
Given~\eqref{eq:n-lb} and~\eqref{eq:frame-values},
for large \( R \) the right-hand side is \( <4\log{Q} e^{-rn/2} \),
and the sum of~\eqref{eq:prob-bd} for all \( n>cR^{2}k^{2} \) is
\begin{align*}
    \le 4\log{Q} \sum_{n>cR^{2}k^{2}}e^{- r n/2}
\le 4(k+1)\logR\cdot e^{-r cR^{2}k^{2}/2}\sum_{n> 0}e^{-rn/2}.
\end{align*}
The multipliers of \( e^{-r c R^{2}k^{2}/2} \) don't change the rate of growth much,
so we can bound the probability by \( \theta_{k} \) as defined in~\eqref{eq:no-birth-prob}.
\end{prooof}                          
\begin{step+}{step:birth.canon}
  Now we repeat the construction above, turning it into a canonical simulation.
\end{step+}
\begin{prooof}
  As we constructed the sequence of cells \( c_{s}=(x_{s},t_{s}) \), \( s=1,2,\dots \),
  the times \( t_{s} \) were chosen on the basis of the trajectory \( \eta \) before \( t_{s} \),
  so these times \( t_{s} \) are stopping times according to Definition~\ref{def:stopping-time}.
  It is not important to upper-bound the number of steps, but \( n^{*}=2T^{\bullet *}/T^{\bullet} \)
  will serve.
  Following the reasoning in part~\ref{step:birth.probab-estim},
  choose in every possible way a subset \( S \) of size \( > n^{*}-4\log{Q} \) of the set
  \( \{1,\dots,n^{*}\} \) of indices.
  Number these subsets as \( S_{1},S_{2},\dots,S_{N} \).
  Subset \( S_{i} \) represents the assumption that the steps \( s\in S_{i} \) are
  the stalling steps.
  In order to define the canonical simulation, we repeat the reasoning of
  part~\ref {step:birth.constr} above.

  Let us fix one of the sets \( S=S_{i} \).
  For each element \( s\in S \) in increasing order,
  let us examine a \emph{presumed} stalling step  starting at time \( t_{s} \),
  at the shorter end of the germ \( G_{s} \) of cell \( c_{s} \).
  Without loss of generality, assume it is the left end.
Let \( u_{1} \) be the start of a growth part of a new work stage
of \( G_{s} \) after \( t_{s} \) (started by the center cell of \( G_{i} \)).
After \( u_{1} \), the germ \( G_{s} \) may grow.
If it reaches \( \rho L_{s} \), or meets a colony cell or a germ cell
with \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{G-size\/}}}}\ge\rho L_{s} \), then \( s \) is not a stalling step: we set
\begin{align}\label{eq:bail-out}
\beta_{S,s}=\omega,\quad W_{i,r}=\emptyset,   
\end{align}
and proceed to \( j+1 \).
We will call this action \emph{bailing out}.
Another possibility is that the left end has reached its farthest possible address,
another that another germ is in the way: one with \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{G-size\/}}}} \) between \( L_{s}/\rho \)
and \( \rho L_{s} \); we already excluded the other possibilities.
In case the left end has reached the farthest address, we will turn attention to the right end, so
without loss of generality, assume that the left end does not reach the farthest address,
because another germ \( G' \) is in the way.
Let \( x_{s} \) be the central cell of \( G_{s} \) and \( x' \) be that of \( C' \).
Now we look at the first \( m=\lambda+2 \) times
\( \tau^{*}_{1},\tau^{*}_{2},\dots \) when \( x_{2} \) or \( x' \)
make random choices, let \( y_{j}\in \{x_{s},x'\} \) be the element making its choice.
For every possible binary sequence \( \mathbf{b} = b_{1},\dots,b_{m} \) we will bail out
unless \( y_{j}=x_{s} \) if and only if \( b_{i}=1 \).
We will also bail out if the choice is \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Dominant\/}}}}(y_{j})=j \) for all \( j \).
Both of these decisions can be made at the last time \( \tau_{m} \), if not earlier.
For the remaining cases,
\begin{align*}
\beta_{S,s,\mathbf{b},j}:=\alpha(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{rand\/}}},f_{j}),\quad W_{S,s}:=W_{0}(y_{j},\tau^{*}_{j}),
\end{align*}
where \( \alpha(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{rand\/}}},d) \) and \( W_{0}(x,t) \) were
defined in Condition~\ref{cond:comput}\ref{i:comput.rand}.
This construction results in the required canonical simulation.
Summing up the non-bailed out bounds results in the same estimate as the more
intuitive one given in parts~\ref{step:birth.constr} and~\ref{step:birth.probab-estim} above.
\end{prooof}

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:sorg}
  For a trajectory $\eta$ of one of the media $M=M_{k}$, of our amplifier, and
  \( \mathcal{E} \) an event depending on the behavior of \( \eta \) before \( t_{1} \).
For a finite or infinite space interval \( H \), assume that 
  \( H':=\Gamma(H,C_{1}{B}^{*}) \) is germ-level blue modulo \( (\sigma,\mathcal{E}) \)
  in \( \eta \) at time $t_{1}$, and let $t_{2}=t_{1}+ C_{2}T^{\bullet *}$.
Let \( \mathcal{E}^{*} \) be the event that \( \mathcal{E} \) holds, or not all (0,1 or 2)
intervals of size \( C_{1}{B}^{*} \) at the ends of \( H' \) are blue in \( \eta \)
at time \( t_{1} \).
Then \( H \) is germ-level blue modulo \( (\sigma^{*},\mathcal{E}^{*}) \) at time \( t_{2} \)
for the trajectory \( \eta^{*}  \) in \( M^{*} \).

name: Self-organization

title: Proof
body_md:
et \( I_{1},\dots,I_{n}\subset H \) be any system of intervals of
size \( C_{1}{B}^{*} \), at distance \( \ge 2 C_{1}{B}^{*} \) from each other.
  We need to bound the probability by \( (\sigma^{*})^{n} \) that \( \neg\mathcal{E}^{*} \) holds
  and none of the intervals \( I_{j} \) are good in \( \eta^{*} \).
  It is sufficient to look at one of these intervals---call it \( I \), with
  \begin{align*}
   I'=\Gamma(I,C_{1}{B}^{*}).
\end{align*}
  Indeed, as the space-time rectangles of the argument
  for all of them are disjoint, and the probability estimates come from a canonical
  simulation, the bounds \( \sigma^{*} \) on the probability will multiply.
  Here is an outline of the argument.
  
  We will work within the space-time rectangle
  \begin{align}\label{eq:sorg-rectangle}
   I' \times (t_{1},t_{1}+ C_{2}T^{\bullet *}].
\end{align}
\begin{itemize}
\item 
  Estimate the probability of the event \( \mathcal{F}_{1} \)
  that damage occurs in the rectangle~\eqref{eq:sorg-rectangle}.
\item Estimate the probability of the event \( \mathcal{F}_{2} \) that at time \( t_{1} \) it is not true
  that the interval \( I' \) is germ-level blue with the possible exclusion of a 
  subinterval \( J \) of size \( C_{1}{B} \).
\item Show that assuming \( \neg(\mathcal{F}_{1}\cup\mathcal{F}_{2}) \),
  except for an event \( \mathcal{F}_{3} \) of probability \( \le\theta \)
  the interval \( I \) turns germ-level blue for \( M^{*} \) by time \( t_{2} \).
\end{itemize}
  
Condition~\ref{cond:restor} (Restoration Property) gives the upper bound 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sorg.q_{1}}
  \operatorname{\mathsf P}(\mathcal{F}_{1})
  \le \frac{3 C_{1}{B}^{*} \cdot  C_{2}T^{\bullet *})}{{B}T^{\bullet}}\varepsilon\le 4 C_{1}C_{2}{Q}{U}'\varepsilon.
\end{equation}
Assuming \( \neg\mathcal{E}^{*} \) implies \( \neg\mathcal{E} \) as well.
Let \( \mathcal{F}_{2} \) be the event that \( \neg\mathcal{E} \) holds and there is no interval
\( J \) of size \( C_{1}{B} \) such that, setting \( J'=\Gamma(J,2 C_{1}{B}) \),
the set \( I\setminus J' \) is blue at time \( t_{1} \).
\begin{step+}{step:sorg.first}
  We have \( \operatorname{\mathsf P}(\mathcal{F}_{2})\le (C_{1}{Q}\sigma)^{2} \).
  \end{step+}
  \begin{pproof}
 Let \(  J_{i} = i C_{1}{B}+\left[0,C_{1}{B}\right) \).
    Under the assumption of \( \neg\mathcal{E} \), which we will omit to write
    in the estimates below,
    for some \( i,h \) with \( |i-h|\ge 4 \), let \( \mathcal{F}_{i,h} \) be the event that neither
\( J_{i} \) nor \( J_{h} \) is germ-level and blue, and both intersect \( I' \)..
The germ-level blueness
of \( \eta \) at time \( t_{1} \) modulo \( \sigma \)
implies \( \operatorname{\mathsf P}(\mathcal{F}_{i,h})\le\sigma^{2} \), and hence
\( \operatorname{\mathsf P}\mathopen\{\mskip 1mu\cmexists i,h: \mathcal{F}_{i,h}\mskip 1mu\mathclose\}\le  (3 C_{1}{Q})^{2}\sigma^{2} \).
If there is no such pair \( i,h \) then it is easy to see that there is an \( i \)
such that \( I\setminus J'_{i} \) is blue.
\end{pproof}                  

\begin{step+}{step:sorg.lift}
  Let \( \mathcal{F}_{3} \) be the event that \( \neg(\mathcal{E}\cup\mathcal{F}_{1}\cup\mathcal{F}_{2}) \) holds
  and \( I \) does not become germ-level blue in \( \eta^{*} \).
  Then \( \operatorname{\mathsf P}(\mathcal{F}_{3})\le\theta\), where \( \theta \) was
  defined in~\eqref{eq:no-birth-prob}.
\end{step+}
\begin{pproof}
  By \( \neg\mathcal{F}_{2} \) there is a \( J \) of size \( C_{1}{B} \) such that 
  \( I'\setminus J \) is germ-level blue at time \( t_{1} \), so
  we invoke Lemma~\ref{lem:color-lift}.
\end{pproof}                 

Summarizing, the probability that under condition \( \neg\mathcal{E} \) the interval \( I \) does
not become blue in \( \eta^{*} \) is bounded by
\begin{align}\label{eq:sorg-sum}
  \operatorname{\mathsf P}(\mathcal{F}_{1}\cup\mathcal{F}_{2}\cup\mathcal{F}_{3})
  \le 4C_{1}C_{2}{Q}{U}'\varepsilon + (C_{1}{Q}\sigma)^{2}+\theta.
\end{align}
Let us show that the latter is \( \le\sigma^{*} \),
using the definitions in~\eqref{eq:sg}, those
in~\eqref{eq:frame-values}, and the inequality~\eqref{eq:exp-error}.
We have, for large enough \( R \) and small enough \( \varepsilon \):
\begin{align*}
   4 C_{1}C_{2}{Q}_{k}{U}'_{k}\varepsilon_{k}&=4C_{1}C_{2}R^{2k+4}k^{2}\varepsilon_{k}
 <\theta_{k}/2,
  \\  (C_{1}{Q}_{k}\sigma_{k})^{2}&= C_{1}^{2}R^{2k+2}e^{-2R k^{2}}
                                  < \theta_{k}/2,
\end{align*}
so~\eqref{eq:sorg-sum} is bounded by \( 2\theta=\sigma^{*} \).

title: Proof
body_md:
he field that will be remembered will be \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Color\/}}}} \).
  For the size \( N \) of our space, let us define the finite or infinite level \( K \):
 \[
  K=\bigvee\mathopen\{\mskip 1mu k : 5{B}_{k} \le N\mskip 1mu\mathclose\}.
 \]
  For a certain value of the field $\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Color\/}}}}$ that we call blue,
we create an initial configuration $\eta^{1}(\cdot,0)$ with
blue latent cells covering the whole space.
Let the trajectories $\eta^{1}$, $\eta^{k}$ be defined as before.
The proof will show that by time \( C_{2}T^{\bullet}_{k} \) the space will be
germ-level blue modulo \( \sigma_{k} \); from this via trickle-down
we will be able to control the probability of any particular space-time point
$(x_{1},t_{1})$ not being blue.

Let \( \mathcal{F}_{1} \) be the event \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Blue\/}}}\ne\eta^{1}(x_{1},t_{1}).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Color\/}}}}^{1} \).   
Eventually, we want to upper-bound \( \operatorname{\mathsf P}(\mathcal{F}_{1}) \).
Let us consider first the case of infinite space, that is \( K=\infty \).
  Let 
 \begin{align*}
   v_{1}   &= t_{1},       & v_{k+1} &= v_{k}-T^{\bullet}_{k+1},
   \\  I_{1} &= \{x_{1}\},&  I_{k+1} &= \Gamma(I_{k}, \lambda{B}_{k+1}),
   \\   u_{1}  &= 0, & u_{k+1} &= u_{k}+C_{2}T^{\bullet}_{k+1}.
 \end{align*}
 By Lemma~\ref{lem:sorg}, for each \( k\le K \),
 in the trajectory \( \eta^{k} \), the whole space
 is germ-level blue at time \( u_{k} \) modulo \( \sigma_{k} \).
Let \( \mathcal{F}_{k} \) be the event that \( I_{k} \) is blue at time \( v_{k} \) in \( \eta^{k} \).

  \begin{step+}{step:sorg.stor.F-k}
    We have \(   \operatorname{\mathsf P}(\mathcal{F}_{k+1}\setminus\mathcal{F}_{k})\stackrel{{}_*}{<} {U}'_{k}{Q}_{k}\varepsilon_{k} \),
    where we used the notation introduced in~\eqref{eq:lem}.
 \end{step+}
  \begin{pproof}
    If damage does not occur in \( \eta^{k} \) in
    \( I_{k+1}\times(v_{k}-({p}_{0}+2)T^{\bullet}_{k+1},v_{k}] \)
    and \( \mathcal{F}_{k+1} \) holds then Lemma~\ref{lem:color-trickle} (Color trickle-down)
    implies \( \mathcal{F}_{k} \).
    The right-hand side above upper-bounds the probability of damage there.
    Now
    \begin{align*}
{U}'_{k}{Q}_{k}\varepsilon_{k} < \varepsilon^{2^{n-2} + 2^{(n-3)/2}}
       <\varepsilon^{2^{n-2}},   
\end{align*}
\end{pproof}                     

  Let
 \begin{align*}
      n = \bigwedge\mathopen\{\verythinmathskipk: v_{k+1} \le u_{k+1} \text{ or } k = K\mskip 1mu\mathclose\},
 \quad t_{2} = u_{n}.
 \end{align*}
If \( K=\infty \) then we always have \( v_{n+1}\le u_{n+1} \), hence
\begin{align*}
 v_{n+1} &=v_{n}-T^{\bullet}_{n+1} \le u_{n+1},\quad u_{n}<v_{n}, 
\\  v_{n} &\le u_{n+1}+T^{\bullet}_{n+1},\quad v_{n}-u_{n}\le(C_{2}+1)T^{\bullet}_{n+1}.
\end{align*}
   Let \(  I' = \Gamma(I_{n}, (C_{2}+1){B}_{n} T^{\bullet} _{n+1}/{T_{\bullet}}_{n}) \).
  Let \( \mathcal{B} \) be the event that \( I' \) is blue in \( \eta^{n} \) at time \( u_{n} \).
  Since \( \eta^{n} \) is blue at time \( u_{n} \) modulo \( \sigma_{n} \) for each
\( n \), we have 
\begin{align*}
 \operatorname{\mathsf P}(\neg\mathcal{B})\stackrel{{}_*}{<} {U}'_{n}\sigma_{n}.
\end{align*}
We claim \(  \operatorname{\mathsf P}(\mathcal{B}\setminus\mathcal{F}_{n})\stackrel{{}_*}{<} ({U}'_{n})^{2}\varepsilon_{n} \).
 Indeed, if damage does not occur in \( \eta^{k} \)  in \( I'\times(u_{n},v_{n}] \)
 then \( \mathcal{B} \) and Lemma~\ref{lem:lasting-color-control} imply \( \mathcal{F}_{n} \).
 And the right-hand side upper-bounds the probability of damage occurring there.  
Thus, 
\begin{align*}
  \operatorname{\mathsf P}(\neg\mathcal{F}_{1})&\le \sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\operatorname{\mathsf P}(\mathcal{F}_{k+1}\setminus\mathcal{F}_{k})
  + \operatorname{\mathsf P}(\neg\mathcal{B})+\operatorname{\mathsf P}(\mathcal{B}\setminus\mathcal{F}_{n}) 
\\ &\stackrel{{}_*}{<} \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} {U}'_{k}{Q}_{k}\varepsilon_{k}
     +{U}'_{n}\sigma_{n} + ({U}'_{n})^{2}\varepsilon_{n}.
\end{align*}
With the parameters of~\eqref{eq:amp-fr}, large enough \( R \)
and small enough \( \varepsilon \) we have
\begin{align*}
     &\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\operatorname{\mathsf P}(\mathcal{F}_{k+1}\setminus\mathcal{F}_{i}) = O(\varepsilon),
\\  &{U}'_{n}\sigma_{n}=R^{n+3}n^{2}e^{-R n^{2}}<e^{-R n^{2}/2},
  \\ &({U}'_{n})^{2}\varepsilon_{n} = R^{2n+6}n^{4}\varepsilon^{2^{n-2} + 2^{(n-3)/2}}
       <\varepsilon^{2^{n-2}},
\end{align*}
for any somewhat large \( n \) and small \( \varepsilon \),
giving \( \operatorname{\mathsf P}(\neg\mathcal{F}_{1})\stackrel{{}_*}{<} e^{-R n^{2}/2}+\varepsilon \).
Let us upper-bound \( e^{-R n^{2}/2} \) by lower-bounding \( n \).
We have
\begin{align*}
   t_{1}\le (C_{2}+1)\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}T^{\bullet}_{k}\stackrel{{}_*}{<} T^{\bullet}_{n+1}.
\end{align*}
From~\eqref{eq:B_k-expl} for large \( k \):
\begin{align*}
  t_{1} &\le T^{\bullet}_{n+1}= R^{(n+2)(n+3)/2-2}(n!)^{2},
  \\  \ln t_{1}&< 0.6 n^{2}\lnR,
  \\  n^{2} &>(1/0.6\lnR) \ln t_{1},
  \\ e^{-R n^{2}}&\le t_{1}^{-R/0.6\lnR},
\end{align*}
which leads to the estimate in Theorem~\ref{thm:1dim.nonerg}.

 \begin{step+}{step:sorg.stor.fin}
  Suppose \( u_{n+1}<v_{n+1} \), hence \( n= K \) and the space is finite.
 \end{step+}
 \begin{prooof}
Given \( {B}_{n}\le N\le 5 {B}_{n} \) and the explicit expression for \( {B}_{n} \)
and  (within constant factor of) \( T^{\bullet}_{n} \)
in~\eqref{eq:B_k-expl}, the estimate for \( \varepsilon_{n} \)
in~\eqref{eq:exp-error} and the definition~\eqref{eq:h_0}, we have for large \( n,N \),
where for a later application we have been a little more generous:
\begin{align}
\nonumber  N &<{B}_{k+1}= R^{(n+1)(n+2)/2-1},
\\\nonumber\log N &< (n+1)^{2}\logR/2,
\\\label{eq:k-explicit}  n-2 &> (\log N)^{1/2}(2/\logR)^{1/2}-4,
\\\nonumber 2^{n-2} &> c^{(\log N)^{1/2}}=h_{0}(N,c) \text{ for an appropriate } c>1,
\\\nonumber \varepsilon_{n} &< \varepsilon^{2^{n-2}} \le \varepsilon^{h_{0}(N,c)}.
\end{align}
  Let \( \mathcal{B} \) be the event that the whole space \( \mathbb{Z}_{N} \) is blue in
  \( \eta^{n} \) at time \( u_{n} \).
Since \( \eta^{n} \) is blue at time \( u_{n} \) modulo \( \sigma_{n} \),
and \( 5{B}_{n+1}>N \), we have
\begin{align*}
 \operatorname{\mathsf P}(\neg\mathcal{B})\stackrel{{}_*}{<} {Q}_{n}\sigma_{n}.
\end{align*}
The event \( \mathcal{B}\setminus \mathcal{F}_{n} \) occurs only if there is any
damage in \( \eta^{n} \) between times \( u_{n} \) and \( v_{n} \).
We can upper-bound the probability of this within a constant factor by
\begin{align*}
  \varepsilon_{n}N t_{1}/{B}_{n}T^{\bullet}_{n} \le \varepsilon_{n} t_{1}/T^{\bullet}_{n}\le \varepsilon_{n}t_{1}
  \le\varepsilon^{h_{0}(N,c)}t_{1},
\end{align*}
which is what Theorem~\ref{thm:1dim.nonerg} states.
\end{prooof}

body_md:
his also proves Theorem~\ref{thm:1dim.comp.finite}, and the remark
  at the last part of the proof also proves Theorem~\ref{thm:1dim.stor.var} for the
  finite space.
  Let \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}} \) be a given standard computing transition function over an alphabet \( \Sigma \).
  Construct an amplifier as in Lemma~\ref{lem:amp} with
  the  transition function \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Pl-trans\/}}}_{1}(\cdot)=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}(\cdot) \).
  This amplifier defines cell body sizes \( {B}_{k} \) for all \( k \).
  Given a string \( \rho\in\Sigma_{0}^{n} \) in the input-output alphabet, let
  \begin{align*}
    l=\bigvee\mathopen\{\verythinmathskipk : {B}_{k}\le n\mskip 1mu\mathclose\}.
  \end{align*}
  Create a germ of cells of \( M_{l} \) covering the space interval \( \left[0,n\right) \),
  with address \( {Q}_{l}/2 \) somewhere inside it.
  Fill its \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Payload\/}}}} \) track first with \( * \), then write over the \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Payload\/}}}}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Input\/}}}} \)
  track the string \( \rho \).
  Now apply consecutively the encodings \( \phi_{*l} \), \( \phi_{*(l-1)} \), \( \dots \),
  to get a string \( \rho_{l} \) of \( \mathbb{S}_{1} \).
  The code \( \psi_{*} \) whose existence is stated in the theorem is defined as
  \( \psi_{*}(\rho)=\rho_{l} \),
  which gives \( n_{l}:=|\rho_{l}|<2n \) as required by the theorem.
  From here, with  \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Init\/}}} \) as in Definition~\ref{def:Init},
 we obtain the initial configuration of \( M_{1} \)
 as \( \eta(\cdot,0)=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Init\/}}}_{\psi_{*}}(\rho) \).
 For readability, we will call the color \( -1 \) ``blue'', color 0 ``white'' and
 color 1 ``red''.
 First, for simplicity, assume that the space is infinite.

By the construction, the interval \( \left[0,n_{l}\right) \) is already an \( l \)-level white germ.
First we will show how the space outside it will also promptly self-organize to level \( l \):
of color blue on the left and red on the right.
From then on, the self-organization continues on the whole space, and
at the same time, the computation in the white germ proceeds reliably,
lifting to a higher level in every step of self-organization.
Finally, the trickle-down argument shows that at any time
the result can be read out at the lowest level.
 
 For \( k=1,2,\ldots \), let
 \begin{align*}
   a_{k}&=\sum_{i=2}^{k}C_{1}{B}_{i},\quad
          v_{k} = \sum_{i=2}^{k}C_{2}T^{\bullet}_{i},
\\ J_{k} &= \left[-a_{k},n_{l}+a_{k}\right),          
\quad  H^{-}_{k}=(-\infty,-a_{k}),\quad H^{+}_{k}=\left[n_{l}+a_{k},\infty\right), 
 \end{align*}
 then \( J_{l}=\left[0,n_{l}\right) \),  \( H^{-}_{1}=(-\infty,0) \).
For \( j=1,2,3 \) let \( \mathcal{A}_{k,j} \) be the event that  in \( \eta^{k} \) at time \( v_{k} \),
the interval \( \left[- j a_{k+1},-a_{k}\right) \) is not germ-level blue or
\( \left[n_{l}- a_{k},n_{l}+ j a_{k+1}\right) \) is not germ-level red.
 Let
\begin{align*}
 \mathcal{D}_{k}=\bigcup_{i= 1}^{k}\mathcal{A}_{i,1}.
\end{align*}
 Note that \( \mathcal{A}_{1,1}=\mathcal{D}_{1}=\emptyset \).
\begin{step+}{step:1dim.comp.outside}
 For each \( k \), in \( \eta^{k} \)  at time \( v_{k} \),
  the set \( H^{-}_{k}\setminus H^{-}_{k+1} \)
  is germ-level blue and \( H^{+}_{l}\setminus H^{+}_{l+1} \) is germ-level red
 modulo \( (\sigma_{k},\mathcal{D}_{k-1}) \).
\end{step+}
   \begin{sloppypar}
 \begin{pproof}
   Interval \( H^{-}_{1} \) is germ-level blue at time \( 0 \) in \( \eta^{1} \) by definition.
Lemma~\ref{lem:sorg} implies that \( H^{-}_{2} \) is germ-level blue in
 \( \eta^{2} \)  at time \( v_{2} \) modulo \( (\sigma_{2},\mathcal{D}_{1}) \), further
\( H^{-}_{3} \) is germ-level blue in
\( \eta^{3} \)  at time \( v_{3} \) modulo \( (\sigma_{3},\mathcal{D}_{2}) \), and so on.
The same argument works for \( H^{+}_{k} \).     
\end{pproof}                         
   \end{sloppypar}

For \( k\ge l \), let \( \mathcal{F}_{k} \)
be the event that there is damage in \( \eta^{k} \) in the space-time rectangle 
\begin{align*}
 \Gamma(J_{l},3 a_{k+1})\times (0,v_{k+1}].
\end{align*}
\begin{step+}{step:1dim.comp.middle}
  Assuming \( \neg \mathcal{F}_{l} \), the interval \( J_{l} \) is part of a white germ
 at time \( v_{l} \) in \( \eta^{l} \).
\end{step+}
\begin{pproof}
 We started from the interval \( J_{l} \) of level \( l \) cells surrounded by level 1 latent cells.
In the absence of  damage in \( \eta^{l} \), these cells perform according to the program,
hence up to time \( v_{l}<2 T^{\bullet}_{l+1} \), none of them would die.
\end{pproof}                        

\begin{step+}{step:1dim.comp.boundary}
From \( \neg(\mathcal{A}_{l,3}\cup\mathcal{F}_{l}) \) follows that in \( \eta^{l} \)
at time \( v_{l}+2T^{\bullet}_{l+1} \),  interval \( J_{l} \) is part of a white germ,
and \( \Gamma(J_{l},2 a_{l+1}) \) is germ-level color-controlled.
\end{step+}
\begin{pproof}
At time \( v_{l} \)  in \( \eta^{l} \), as part~\ref{step:1dim.comp.middle} shows,
  \( \neg\mathcal{F}_{l} \) implies that  \( J_{l} \) is part of a white germ.
And \( \neg\mathcal{A}_{l,3} \), implies by definition that
\( \left[-3 a_{l+1},-a_{l}\right) \) is germ-level blue and
\( \left[n_{l}-a_{l},n_{l}+3 a_{l+1}\right) \) is germ-level red.
We can now apply the argument of Lemma~\ref{lem:robust-color-control}
simultaneously with 
with \( I=\left[-3 a_{l+1},n_{l}\right) \),  \( J=\left[-a_{l},0\right) \),
and with \( I=\left[0,n_{l}+3 a_{l+1}\right) \), \( J=\left[n_{l},n_{l}+a_{l}\right) \),
to imply that in \( \eta^{l} \) at time \( v_{l}+2T^{\bullet}_{l+1} \),
the whole interval \( \Gamma(J_{l},2 a_{l+1}) \) becomes germ-level color-controlled.
\end{pproof}                               

\begin{step+}{step:1dim.comp.next}
From \( \neg(\mathcal{A}_{l,3}\cup\mathcal{F}_{l}) \) follows that in \( \eta^{l+1} \)
at time \( v_{l+1} \), the interval \( J_{l} \) is part of a white germ,
and interval \( \Gamma(J_{l},a_{l+1}) \) is germ-level color-controlled,
 except for an event \( \mathcal{E}_{l} \) of probability
\begin{align*}
   \le (2 C_{1}+7)\theta_{l},
\end{align*}
where \( \theta_{l} \)  was defined in~\eqref{eq:no-birth-prob}.
\end{step+}
\begin{pproof}
  From \( \mathcal{F}_{l} \) follows that \( J_{l} \) is part of a white germ also in
  \( \eta^{l+1} \).
By part~\ref{step:1dim.comp.boundary},
from \( \neg(\mathcal{A}_{l,3}\cup\mathcal{F}_{l}) \) follows that in \( \eta^{l} \) at time
\( v_{l}+2T^{\bullet}_{l+1} \),
the interval \( \Gamma(J_{l},2 a_{l+1}) \) is germ-level color-controlled.
Note that \( v_{l+1}=v_{l}+2T^{\bullet}_{l+1}+26{p}_{0}T^{\bullet}_{l+1} \).
Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:color-lift}, for case \( \eta=\eta^{l} \),
\( t_{2}-t_{1}=26{p}_{0}T^{\bullet}_{l+1} \),
to any subinterval \( K \) of length \( 2{B}_{l+1} \) of \( \Gamma(J_{l},a_{l+1}) \),
we find that \( K \) becomes color-controlled in \( \eta^{l+1} \) except for
an event of probability \( \theta_{l} \).
If each of the \( r \)  intervals of the form
\( \left[i{B}_{l+1},(i+2){B}_{l+1}\right) \) 
intersecting \( \Gamma(J_{l},a_{l+1}) \) becomes color-controlled then so does
\( \left[-a_{l+1},n_{l}-a_{l+1}\right) \).
Let \( \mathcal{E}_{l} \) be the event that any one of them does not become color-controlled,
then \( \operatorname{\mathsf P}(\mathcal{E}_{l})\le r\theta_{l} \).
The construction gave \( |J_{l}|<5 {B}_{l+1} \),
we know \( a_{l+1}<2C_{1}{B}_{l+1} \), hence
\( |\Gamma(J_{l},a_{l+1})|< (4 C_{1}+5){B}_{l+1} \), \( r\le 4 C_{1}+9 \).
\end{pproof}                      

Let us handle now first the case of infinite space \( \mathbb{Z} \).

\begin{step+}{step:1dim.comp.above}
  Let \( k>l \).
  Assume that in \( \eta^{k} \) at time \( v_{k} \)
the interval \( J_{l} \) is part of a white germ, and
the interval \( \Gamma(J_{l},a_{k}) \) is germ-level color-controlled.
Then from \( \neg(\mathcal{A}_{k,2}\cup\mathcal{F}_{k}) \) follows that in \( \eta^{k+1} \)
at time \( v_{k+1} \), the interval \( J_{l} \) is part of a white germ,
and interval \( \Gamma(J_{l},a_{k+1}) \) is germ-level color-controlled,
 except for an event \( \mathcal{E}_{k} \) of probability \( \le (2 C_{1}+3)\theta_{k} \).
\end{step+}
\begin{pproof}
  (This proof is similar to the one above.)
    From \( \mathcal{F}_{k} \) follows that \( J_{l} \) is part of a white germ also in
  \( \eta^{k+1} \).
  From \( \neg\mathcal{A}_{k,2} \) follows that in \( \eta^{l} \) at time \( v_{l} \)
also the interval \( \Gamma(J_{l},2 a_{k+1}) \) is germ-level color-controlled.
 Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:color-lift}, for case \( \eta=\eta^{k} \),
\( t_{2}-t_{1}=C_{2}T^{\bullet}_{k+1} \),
to any subinterval \( K \) of length \( 2{B}_{k+1} \) of \( \Gamma(J_{l},a_{k+1}) \),
we find that \( K \) becomes color-controlled in \( \eta^{k+1} \) except for
an event of probability \( \theta_{k} \).
If each of the \( r \)  intervals of the form \( \left[i{B}_{k+1},(i+2){B}_{k+1}\right) \) 
intersecting \( \Gamma(J_{l},a_{l+1}) \) becomes color-controlled then so does
\( \Gamma(J_{l},a_{l+1}) \).
Let \( \mathcal{E}_{k} \) be the event that any one of them does not become color-controlled;
then \( \operatorname{\mathsf P}(\mathcal{E}_{k})\le r\theta_{k} \).
The construction gave \( |J_{l}|<{B}_{k+1} \),
we know \( a_{k+1}<2C_{1}{B}_{k+1} \), hence
\( |\Gamma(J_{l},a_{l+1})|< (4 C_{1}+1){B}_{l+1} \), \( r\le 4 C_{1}+5 \).
\end{pproof}                       

For \( k\ge l \) let
\begin{align*}
   \mathcal{D}'_{k} = \bigcup_{i=l}^{k}\mathcal{A}_{l,2}, \quad
  \mathcal{G}_{k}=\mathcal{D}_{l-1}\cup\mathcal{A}_{l,3}\cup\mathcal{D}'_{k-1}\cup\bigcup_{i=l}^{k-1}\mathcal{F}_{i}
           \cup\bigcup_{i=l}^{k-1}\mathcal{E}_{i},
\end{align*}
where the events \( \mathcal{E}_{i} \) were defined in the proofs of part~\ref{step:1dim.comp.next}
and part~\ref{step:1dim.comp.above}.

\begin{step+}{step:1dim.comp.combine}
  Let \( k> l \).
  Assuming \( \neg\mathcal{G}_{k} \), in \( \eta^{l+1} \) at time \( v_{l+1} \)
the interval \( \Gamma(J_{l},a_{k}) \) is germ-level color-controlled,
and the interval \( J_{l} \) is part of a white germ.
Also,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:G-bound}
\begin{aligned}
  \operatorname{\mathsf P}(\mathcal{G}_{k})&\le 2\sum_{i=1}^{l-1}{Q}_{i}\sigma_{i}+6{Q}_{l}\sigma_{l}
                  + 4\sum_{i=l}^{k-1}{Q}_{i}\sigma_{i}
  \\ &+ 33\sum_{i=l}^{k-1}{Q}_{i}{U}'_{i}\varepsilon_{i}
       +  (2 C_{1}+7)\theta_{l} + \sum_{i=l+1}^{k-1}(4 C_{1}+5)\theta_{i}=O(\sigma_{1}).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
\end{step+}
\begin{pproof}
  The statement before the probability estimate,
  for \( k=l+1 \), follows from part~\ref{step:1dim.comp.next}.
  For \( k>l+1 \), it follows by induction from part~\ref{step:1dim.comp.above}.
  It remains to prove \eqref{eq:G-bound}.
From the definition, \( \mathcal{D}_{k}=\bigcup_{i=2}^{k}(\mathcal{A}_{i,1}\setminus\mathcal{D}_{i-1}) \).  
From
\begin{align*}
  \operatorname{\mathsf P}(\mathcal{A}_{i+1,j}\setminus\mathcal{A}_{i,j})&\le 2 j {Q}_{k}\sigma_{k}
\end{align*}
we have
\(  \operatorname{\mathsf P}(\mathcal{D}_{k})\le 2\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}{Q}_{i}\sigma_{i} \),
\(  \operatorname{\mathsf P}(\mathcal{D}'_{k})\le 4\sum_{i=l}^{k-1}{Q}_{i}\sigma_{i} \).                     
Given \( n_{l}<5{B}_{l+1} \),
\( a_{k+1}< 2{B}_{k+1} \),  \( v_{k+1}\le 2T^{\bullet}_{k+1} \), we have
\begin{align*}
  \operatorname{\mathsf P}(\mathcal{F}_{k})\le 11 ({B}_{k+1}/{B}_{k})\cdot 2(T^{\bullet}_{k+1}/T^{\bullet}_{k})
  \le 33 {Q}_{k}{U}'_{k}\varepsilon_{k}.
\end{align*}
The estimates for \( \mathcal{E}_{k} \) were given in parts~\ref{step:1dim.comp.next} 
and~\ref{step:1dim.comp.above}.
\end{pproof}                         

In the reasoning below, we assume \( \neg\mathcal{G}_{k} \).
Between times \( v_{k} \) and \( v_{k+1} \), we have a white germ
containing \( J_{l} \), around the germ cell with address \( {Q}_{k}/2 \).
Besides lifting from level \( k \) to level \( k+1 \),
the trajectory \( \eta^{k} \) performs its payload computation;
for each level \( i\le k \), this proceeds without faults
up to time \( v_{i+1} \), in the area \( \Gamma(J_{l},a_{i+1}) \)
which is all the area that matters, as the germ does not grow beyond it.
But we are interested in the output of level \( 1 \), so trickle-down will be invoked.
According to the rules \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Compute\/}}}} \) of Algorithm~\ref{alg:Compute} and
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Update-payload\/}}}} \) of Algorithm~\ref{alg:Update-payload},
payload computation happens on level \( k \)
representing germ cells of level \( k+1 \) with addresses in \( \left[0,{Q}_{k+1}\right) \).
We will estimate the number of payload computation steps performed, but first assume that
time \( t' \) is the end of a dwell period of a germ cell \( x' \) of \( \eta^{k} \),
in which \( x=x'+a \) for some \( a\in\left[0,{B}_{k}\right) \),
and \( \eta^{k}(x',t').\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Payload\/}}}}(a) \) is supposed to have the value \( \zeta(x,t) \).
Under the assumption \( \neg\mathcal{G}_{k} \) indeed
\( \zeta(x,t)=\eta^{k}(x', t').\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Payload\/}}}}(a) \).
A trickle-down reasoning just like in Section~\ref{sec:trickle-down}, in the proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:remember-inf}, with \( D_{k}=T^{\bullet}_{k} \), as done for
information storage in the discussion after Lemma~\ref{lem:amp} (Amplifier),
will bring the equality down to level 1:
\begin{align*}
  \operatorname{\mathsf P}\mathopen\{\mskip 1mu\zeta(x,t).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Output\/}}}}\ne \eta(x, t').\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Output\/}}}}\mskip 1mu\mathclose\}&\le\operatorname{\mathsf P}(\mathcal{G}_{k})+
                                                    \varepsilon_{k}+\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}\varepsilon''_{i}
\\ &= O(\sigma_{1})=O(e^{-R}).
\end{align*}

Let us now estimate \( t' \) in terms of \( t \).
Let \( t'_{k} \) be the time by which the first white cell of \( M_{k} \)
will be created, then we have \( v_{k-1}< t'_{k} \le v_{k} \).
Between times \( t'_{k} \) and \( t'_{k+1} \), 
there are enough computation steps to simulate in \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}} \)
the \( {B}_{k+1}-{B}_{k} \) steps of the expansion of an area of
size \( {B}_{k} \) to one of size \( {B}_{k+1} \).
This shows that if \( {B}_{k}< t \le {B}_{k+1} \) then
\( t_{k}\le t'<t_{k+1} \).
Recall the definition of bandwidth \( w_{k} \) in~\eqref{eq:amp-fr}.
During the time interval \( (t'_{k},t'_{k+1}] \), starting at time \( t'_{k} \)
until the payload of a germ of size \( {B}_{k+1} \) is filled,
each work period of a germ cell simulates at least a constant times
\( w_{k}{B}_{k} \) steps of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}} \).
So if \( t>{B}_{k} \) then to simulate \( t \) steps of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}} \) we need,
within constant factor,
\( t/{B}_{k}w_{k} \) work periods, each of length \( \leT^{\bullet}_{k} \), so 
\begin{align*}
   t T^{\bullet}_{k}/{B}_{k}w_{k}.
\end{align*}
For \( t\le{B}_{k} \) we need less, so we are conservative when going with this
estimate for all \( t \).
Noting that \( \prod_{i<k}{U}'_{i} \) is within constant factor of \( T^{\bullet}_k \),
and using~\eqref{eq:B_k-expl}, we have within constant factor
\begin{align*}
   T^{\bullet}_{k}/{B}_{k}w_{k} = R^{k}(k!)^{2}< 2^{2.1  k\log k}.
\end{align*}
Using~\eqref{eq:B_k-expl} we have for large \( t \),
\begin{align}
  \nonumber
  t&>B_{k}=R^{k(k+1)/2-1},
\\\nonumber \log t &> \logR\cdot k^{2}/2,
  \\\label{eq:k-bound}  k &< (\log t)^{1/2}(2/\logR)^{1/2},
\\\nonumber    2^{2.1 k\log k} &< c^{ (\log t)^{1/2}\log\log t},
\end{align}
for a constant \( c \) depending on \( R \).
So we can estimate \( t'\le t\cdot c^{(\log t)^{1/2}\log\log t} \)
as Theorem~\ref{thm:1dim.comp} states.

In case of the finite space \( \mathbb{Z}_{N} \) we can only hope to simulate the
computation \( \zeta(\cdot,t) \) while it fits into a space of size \( N \),
so let
\begin{align*}
   K = \bigvee\mathopen\{\verythinmathskipk : B_{k}< N\mskip 1mu\mathclose\}.
\end{align*}
\begin{step+}{step:1dim.comp.finite}
  In case of a space \( \mathbb{Z}_{N} \) for finite \( N \), adding \( \varepsilon^{h_{0}(N,c)}t \)
  to the estimate with a constant \( c>1 \) will do.
  The same argument works also to finish the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:1dim.stor.var}
  for a finite space.
\end{step+}
\begin{pproof}
  After the level has been raised to \( K \), it will not be raised any longer.
  In every time period of size  \( T^{\bullet}_{K} \), the computation may fail
  if a fault of level \( K \) occurs, that is with probability \( \varepsilon_{K} \).
  In time \( t \) the probability of this happening at least once can be (generously)
  be upper-bounded by \( \varepsilon_{K}t \).
  We estimate, similarly to~\eqref{eq:k-explicit}, for \( k=K \):
  \begin{align*}
 \varepsilon_{K} &< \varepsilon^{h_{0}(N,c)}
\end{align*}
for an appropriate \( c>1 \).
\end{pproof}

body_md:
\index{contact process}
  The contact process is a one-dimensional \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CCA\/}}} \) as defined in 
Section~\ref{sec:Markov}.
  Let us note that this this process is not noisy: not all local
transition rates are positive.
  The process has states 0,1.
  In trajectory \( \eta(x,t) \), state \( \eta(x,t)=1 \) turns into 0 with
rate 1.  
  State \( \eta(x,t)=0 \) turns into 1 with rate
\( \lambda(\eta(x-1,t)+\eta(x+1,t)) \).
  It is known that this process has a critical rate\index{critical rate}
\( \lambda_{c}\in(0,\infty) \) with the following properties.
  
  If \( \lambda\le \lambda_{c} \) then the process is mixing with the invariant
measure concentrated on the configuration \( \xi \) with \( \xi(x)=0 \) for
all \( x \).
  If \( \lambda>\lambda_{c} \) then the process is non-ergodic.

  If \( \lambda<\lambda_{c} \) then it is known (see Theorem 3.4 in Chapter VI 
of~\cite{Liggett85}) that the order of magnitude of \( r_{\infty}(n,\delta) \) 
is \( \log n \).

  If \( \lambda=\lambda_{c} \) then the convergence is much slower, with an order
of magnitude that is a power of \( n \) (see Theorem 3.10 in Chapter VI
of~\cite{Liggett85} and \cite{BezuidenhoutGrimmett90}).
